Weekly Family Update – 
02.10.26 
Headteacher’s Update: Keeping You Informed About What Matters Most 
What a fantastic week it has been at Abbey College. I continue to be impressed by our 
students’ positive attitude, hard work and commitment to making a difference to both 
themselves and those around them. 
A particular highlight was our Year 6 Open Evening, where we welcomed over 300 families to 
the college. It was wonderful to see so many prospective students and parents exploring our 
school. Our students were exceptional ambassadors, proudly sharing their experiences and 
helping visitors see what makes Abbey College such a special place. 
A special mention must go to Evie in Year 7, who spoke brilliantly about her first four weeks 
at Abbey College. Her confidence, warmth and engaging delivery captivated the audience, 
and she represented the school exceptionally well. She should be incredibly proud of herself 
and has a very bright future ahead. 
I would also like to thank our Parents' Forum for the outstanding support they provide to our 
school community. Their fundraising and commitment have helped us introduce initiatives 
such as our mobile phone pouches and pre-loved uniform shop, both of which have made a 
real difference to families and students. 
The first Parents' Forum meeting of the year will take place on Wednesday 7 October, 
5.00pm-6.00pm, and all parents and carers are warmly invited to attend. Whether you 
would like to get involved regularly or simply find out more, you will be very welcome. The 
Forum's first fundraising event, a Family Quiz Night, will take place on Thursday 12 
November. We hope many families will be able to join us for what promises to be a fun 
evening. 
Have a wonderful weekend. 
Andy Christoforou, Headteacher 

 
Please read on for essential updates. 
Vacancies at Abbey College and across the Meridian Trust 
https://www.abbey.college/vacancies  
Celebration of Spirit - Recognition 
Year 7 Spirit Lunch 
For the first time ever, Year 7 have a 'Spirit Lunch' built into their 
curriculum. Once a fortnight, students come together to build 
their sense of community by sharing lunch, serving one another, 
and engaging in interesting discussion topics. 
This week's question for discussion was: "If you were elected to rule the world for a day, 
what rule would you change?" 

The answers focused on ending discrimination and caring for those less fortunate, responses 
that truly embodied the Abbey College Spirit. 
Headteacher Commendations w/c 28/09/26 
The following students have been awarded with Headteacher's Commendations this week 
for going above and beyond in an area of school life.  They will receive 10 Spirit points and a 
special postcard home. 
 

 
Staff member of the week 
Mr Valentine: Intuition: For taking on a completely different challenge and making a real 
difference with the students. Every day is different in New Horizons, and you just go with it 
and have shown a calm and caring nature towards the students they really respond to. 
Thank you for all your hard work and support to help support them. 
Tell us about something brilliant! 
If you would like to nominate someone for an Abbey College Spirit Award for any out of 
school success stories, then please follow this link or email the Office office@abbey.college. 
Strong Partnerships 
Parent's Forum 
Date for your diary! 
The date of the next Parent's Forum meeting is Wednesday 
7th October 5-6pm. You can either join in person in the 
Boardroom or online via Teams. 
Parent Questionnaire 
Please complete our parent questionnaire to raise any questions you have prior to the next 
meeting. The questionnaire closes on Monday 5th 
October:  https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/ParentsForum26-27 
• Please email ParentsForum@abbey.college any questions.  
• Please find our minutes here: https://www.abbey.college/parents-forum  
• If you would like further information on the Parent's Forum, please email: 
ParentsForum@abbey.college   
Genevieve Wardle - Chair of Parent's Forum 

Uniform Update: Optional Plain Black V-Neck Jumper 
To provide greater flexibility for families whilst maintaining our high uniform standards, 
students may now wear a plain black V-neck jumper under their blazer. 
Please note that: 
• The jumper must be plain black, with no logos, branding, patterns, or 
embellishments. 
• It must be V-necked to allow the school tie and shirt collar to remain visible. 
• Hoodies, sweatshirts, crew-neck jumpers, or knitwear in other colours are not 
permitted. 
• The jumper must be worn underneath the blazer, not as an alternative to it. 
Family Quiz Night! 
The Abbey College Parents' Forum invites families to a fun-filled Family Quiz Night on 
Thursday 12th November in the South Hall. 
Gather a team of up to six people, test your knowledge, and compete for prizes, all while 
supporting a great cause. Every penny raised will go towards exciting new opportunities and 
resources for Abbey College students. 
 

Up-to-date MCAS details 
Please ensure that your contact details are kept up to date on MCAS (MyChildAtSchool). 
Having the correct information helps us contact you quickly if needed and ensures you 
receive important school communications. 
You can update your details yourself at any time through the MCAS app or website. 
Alternatively, if you need assistance, please email office@abbey.college with your updated 
information. 
Zebra Crossing location Survey 
The County Council would like feedback on a proposed Zebra Crossing location near the 
school. Please complete the survey here: https://yourvoice.cambridgeshire.gov.uk/place-
and-sustainability/ramsey-zebra-crossing-feedback/ 
Any queries, please contact Hanane Rouadi, Assistant Project Manager, Local Improvements 
Team, Hanane.Rouadi@cambridgeshire.gov.uk 
Diary Dates  
 
Everything You Need to Know About Assessments 
 

Ensuring Pupils Feel Safe and Behave Well 
Safety First 
Worries 
Students discussed emotional wellbeing and the importance of talking about worries early. 
They were reminded of the support available in school and encouraged to seek help if they 
are struggling. 
Useful Resources 
• YoungMinds: https://www.youngminds.org.uk/parent 
• Anna Freud: https://www.annafreud.org/parents-and-carers 
• Place2Be: https://parentingsmart.place2be.org.uk 
• NHS Every Mind Matters: https://www.nhs.uk/every-mind-matters 
If you need support or have any concerns about your child's wellbeing or safety, please 
contact welfare@abbey.college 
Promoting Positive Behaviour Every Day 
Student attendance  
Week 4 – Impact on Wellbeing  
Being in school supports more than just your learning—it supports your wellbeing too.  
Routine, friendships, and feeling part of your community all help you feel positive and 
confident.  
Coming in matters for your mind as well as your grades.  

Supporting Your Child’s Wider Development 
Offer & Opportunity Programme (OOPs) - Autumn Term 
 
 

 
Student curriculum 
How can I find out what my child is learning in each subject? 
Discover Our Curriculum 
At Abbey College, we want every student to feel challenged, supported and inspired to 
achieve their best. Our broad and balanced curriculum combines excellent teaching, rich 
experiences and strong careers guidance to help young people thrive both in school and 
beyond. 
Our curriculum is designed around three simple aims: helping students understand the 
wider world, providing an ambitious education for all, and ensuring that every learner has 
the opportunity to succeed. Parents can explore what is taught across Key Stages 3, 4 and 5, 
along with information about homework, higher-attaining students and relationships 
education. 
Find out more: View our Curriculum Overview 
Communicating with us and raising concerns 
Click here to access this Communication Flowchart on our website. 
Parent Friendly Policy Guide: 
https://www.abbey.college/key-policies--reports  
Other news updates can be found here: 
• Our news page: https://www.abbey.college/school-communications  
• Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/pg/RamseyAbbeyCollege/posts/  
• Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/abbeycollege_ramsey/

Weekly Family Update - 09.10.26 
Headteacher’s Update: Keeping You Informed About What Matters 
Most 
Thank you for your continued support in helping your child attend school every day. Regular 
attendance is one of the most important factors in a young person's success, wellbeing and 
sense of belonging at school. 
Every lesson matters. Being in school each day helps students build strong relationships, 
develop confidence, keep up with learning and make the most of the opportunities available 
to them. Even missing occasional days can make it harder for students to stay connected to 
their learning. 
As we approach the half-term break, we would be grateful for your support in ensuring 
students attend every day until the end of term. Students finish for half term on Thursday 22 
October. 
Please note that the following are Meridian Trust INSET days, when students are not in 
school: 
• Friday 23 October 
• Monday 2 November 
This means students will have an extended break before returning to school on Tuesday 3 
November, giving plenty of time to rest and recharge. 
Thank you for working with us to ensure students are in school, on time, every day. Your 
support makes a real difference. 
Every day in school is a day of learning, friendship and opportunity. 
Andy Christoforou, Headteacher 

 
Please read on for essential updates. 
Vacancies at Abbey College and across the Meridian Trust 
https://www.abbey.college/vacancies  
Celebration of Spirit - Recognition 
 

Headteacher Commendations w/c 05/10/26 
The following students have been awarded with Headteacher's Commendations this week 
for going above and beyond in an area of school life.  They will receive 10 Spirit points and a 
special postcard home. 

 

 
Staff member of the week 
Miss Andrew-Martin: Passion - Your love for creative writing is infectious. To have 30 
students regularly attending an OOP and being so proud of the work they produce there is 
wonderful to see. Thank you for being so willing to give up your time to allow students to 
feel such a sense of pride and belonging. 
Tell us about something brilliant! 

If you would like to nominate someone for an Abbey College Spirit Award for any out of 
school success stories, then please follow this link or email the Office office@abbey.college . 
Strong Partnerships 
Parent's Forum 
Parent's Forum Update 
At last night’s Parent's Forum meeting, Mrs Noble provided an overview of the changes to 
the Relationships and Sex Education (RSE) guidance and invited feedback from parents. If 
you would like to contribute, please submit any comments here:  
• Relationships, Sex and Health Education: Parent Consultation – Fill in form.  
We look forward to using your feedback to help shape our updated policy, which will be 
published next year. 
We also continued planning for our exciting fundraising quiz on 12th November, and 
preparations are well underway. 
At our next Parent's Forum meeting, Miss Lane will provide an update on how our new Year 
7 students are settling into life at Abbey College and we will look at some projects to donate 
funds to. 
• Please email ParentsForum@abbey.college any questions.  
• Please find our minutes here: https://www.abbey.college/parents-forum  
• If you would like further information on the Parent's Forum, please email: 
ParentsForum@abbey.college   
Genevieve Wardle - Chair of Parent's Forum 
Family Quiz Night! 
The Abbey College Parents' Forum invites families to a fun-filled Family Quiz Night on 
Thursday 12th November in the South Hall. 
Gather a team of up to six people for £6 per team, test your knowledge, and compete for 
prizes, all while supporting a great cause.  
There are prizes which have been donated for a raffle on the night.    

The sixth form will be running the quiz so any support would be much appreciated! 
Every penny raised will go towards exciting new opportunities and resources for Abbey 
College students. 
 
Up-to-date MCAS details 
Please ensure that your contact details are kept up to date on MCAS (MyChildAtSchool). 
Having the correct information helps us contact you quickly if needed and ensures you 
receive important school communications. 

You can update your details yourself at any time through the MCAS app or website. 
Alternatively, if you need assistance, please email office@abbey.college with your updated 
information. 
Road Safety 
 
Zebra Crossing location Survey 
The County Council would like feedback on a proposed Zebra Crossing location near the 
school. Please complete the survey here: https://yourvoice.cambridgeshire.gov.uk/place-
and-sustainability/ramsey-zebra-crossing-feedback/ 
Any queries, please contact Hanane Rouadi, Assistant Project Manager, Local Improvements 
Team, Hanane.Rouadi@cambridgeshire.gov.uk 
Diary Dates  
 
��� Inset Days Coming Up 
Please note that the following are Meridian Trust-wide Inset Days. All Meridian Trust 
schools, including Abbey College, will be closed to students on these dates: 
������������ Friday 23 October 
������������Monday 2 November 

������������Friday 27 November 
���� Please add these dates to your family calendar. 
These training days allow staff from across Meridian Trust to work together, share best 
practice and continue to improve the education we provide for all students. 
Everything You Need to Know About Assessments 
 
Ensuring Pupils Feel Safe and Behave Well 
Safety First 
Healthy Habits 
This week students discussed healthy habits, hygiene, hydration, sleep and self-care. 
We encouraged students to consider how everyday health habits support both wellbeing 
and school attendance. 
Useful Resources 
• NHS Live Well: https://www.nhs.uk/live-well 
• NHS Better Health: https://www.nhs.uk/better-health 
• The Sleep Charity: https://thesleepcharity.org.uk 
If you need support or have any concerns about your child's wellbeing or safety, please 
contact welfare@abbey.college 
Promoting Positive Behaviour Every Day 
Student attendance  
Week 5 – Coughs & Colds  

It’s okay to feel under the weather sometimes—but most coughs and colds don’t need days 
off school.  
If you’re well enough, being in school helps you stay on track.  
Don’t let a small illness lead to big gaps in learning.  
Ms Davis – Attendance Officer 
Supporting Your Child’s Wider Development 
Offer & Opportunity Programme (OOPs) - Autumn Term 
 

 
 
 
Click here 
Student curriculum 
How can I find out what my child is learning in each subject? 
Learning outside the classroom (LoTC) 
At Abbey College, we believe learning should extend beyond the classroom. Through a wide 
range of opportunities, students can experience art, culture, heritage, adventure and the 
natural world, helping to broaden their horizons and build confidence. These enriching 
experiences are offered through our curriculum and our Offer and Opportunity Programme 
(OOP), alongside trips, visits and activities such as the Combined Cadet Force (CCF). The aim 
is to give every student access to memorable experiences that support their personal growth 
and development.  
Find out more: Learning Outside the Classroom 
Communicating with us and raising concerns 
Click here to access this Communication Flowchart on our website. 

Parent Friendly Policy Guide: 
https://www.abbey.college/key-policies--reports  
Other news updates can be found here: 
• Our news page: https://www.abbey.college/school-communications  
• Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/pg/RamseyAbbeyCollege/posts/  
• Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/abbeycollege_ramsey/

metadata.title: £500,000-funded community hall opens after six years of planning
metadata.contentSnippet: A new community hall has opened in Fenstanton, Cambridgeshire, following more than six years of planning.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £500,000-funded community hall opens after six years of planning
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A new community hall has opened in Fenstanton, Cambridgeshire, following more than six years of planning. Fenstanton Community Hall, located on Crest Drive, officially opened on September 30 and aims to offer a welcoming, fully accessible space for residents of all ages. The project received a £500,000 contribution from Cambridgeshire County Council. Peter McDonald, Chair of Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "Community spaces like this can be truly transformational. New Fenstanton Community Hall (Image: Cambridgeshire County Council) "We know from our Quality of Life Survey that loneliness remains an important issue for many people, and places where residents can come together, take part in activities and build relationships are more valuable than ever. "Cambridgeshire County Council has been proud to support this project over a number of years, from providing £500,000 in funding to helping bring partners together to make it happen. "The new hall is a great example of what can be achieved through collaboration, creating a lasting resource that will benefit residents for many years to come." The facility includes a multi-purpose hall, kitchen, IT hub, flexible meeting spaces, and accommodation for the parish council. Kevin Forbes Mitchell, trustee of the Fenstanton Village Hall Trust, said: "After more than six years of planning, fundraising and seeing the building grow from an idea into reality, it's fantastic to finally open the doors. Former Fenstanton Village Hall (Image: Cambridgeshire County Council) "The hall has been designed as a place for everyone, whether that's attending a fitness class, joining a book club, using the digital hub, coming to a community event or simply dropping in for a coffee and a chat. "We hope it becomes a real hub for village life and a place where people can connect and enjoy spending time together." Activities planned for the hall include martial arts, music, weddings, exhibitions, and business events, aiming to meet the rising demand for accessible community space in the growing village.

metadata.title: Photos show scale of £200k cannabis haul found in back of overweight van
metadata.contentSnippet: Photos have captured the scale of a cannabis haul worth £200,000 which was discovered after police stopped an overweight van in Sawtry.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Photos show scale of £200k cannabis haul found in back of overweight van
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Photos have captured the scale of a cannabis haul worth £200,000 which was discovered after police stopped an overweight van. Officers from the spotted the white Mercedes Sprinter box van travelling southbound on the A1 at Norman Cross on March 2. Cannabis worth £200,000 as well as the remnants of a cannabis factory was discovered (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) The van was pulled over at the nearby DVSA weighbridge in Sawtry. Passenger Gjok Ndrevetaj told officers it was carrying commercial waste. However, a check in the back of the vehicle uncovered eight boxes containing cannabis with a street value of up to £200,000. Gjok Ndrevetaj was sentenced to three years and four months in prison (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Plant pots, soil, clippings and heating equipment boxes were also discovered. Ndrevetaj, 33, of Heygate Avenue, Southend, appeared at Huntingdon Law Courts on Tuesday (October 20). He was sentenced to three years and four months in prison after previously pleading guilty to being concerned in the supply of cannabis. Plant pots, soil, clippings and heating equipment boxes were also discovered (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Detective Constable Natalia Bochnacka, who investigated, said: "This case highlights how a routine stop for an overweight vehicle can uncover much more serious criminality. "The discovery of the cannabis alongside the remnants of a cannabis factory demonstrates the scale of the operation. "We are committed to disrupting the supply of illegal drugs and bringing those responsible before the courts." Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: 6 locations in Cambridgeshire with surprising royal connections
metadata.contentSnippet: From Tudor queens and medieval kings to the birthplace of Richard III, Cambridgeshire is packed with places hiding remarkable royal connections.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 6 locations in Cambridgeshire with surprising royal connections
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From Tudor queens and medieval kings to the birthplace of Richard III, Cambridgeshire is packed with locations hiding remarkable royal connections. These towns and villages have played surprising roles in some of the most dramatic chapters of British royal history. Ely’s royal connection stretches back more than 1,300 years. The city was founded around the monastery established by St Etheldreda, daughter of King Anna of East Anglia, in the seventh century. The religious settlement she created grew into one of the most important ecclesiastical centres in medieval England. Royal links continued through the centuries, with members of England’s royal families supporting the cathedral and its diocese. The city’s origins are inseparable from Anglo-Saxon royalty, making Ely one of Cambridgeshire’s oldest royal-associated settlements. Peterborough boasts one of the most remarkable royal connections anywhere in the East of England. Peterborough Cathedral is the final resting place of Catherine of Aragon, the first wife of Henry VIII and a former Queen of England. Following her death at nearby Kimbolton Castle in January 1536, she was buried in what was then Peterborough Abbey. The cathedral later also housed the remains of Mary, Queen of Scots, after her execution at Fotheringhay in 1587, before they were moved to Westminster Abbey by her son, James I. For a period, Peterborough held the graves of two of the most famous women in British royal history. The quiet village of Kimbolton is forever linked to one of the most dramatic chapters in Tudor history. Kimbolton Castle became the final home of Catherine of Aragon after Henry VIII rejected her as queen. Removed from court and increasingly isolated, she spent her last years at the castle before dying there in January 1536. Her death marked the end of a bitter royal dispute that contributed to England’s break with Rome and the English Reformation. Today the castle houses Kimbolton School, but its royal associations remain a major part of its identity. Buckden Towers was once a favoured residence of the powerful Bishops of Lincoln and hosted several monarchs. Henry VIII stayed here during the years leading up to his divorce from Catherine of Aragon, and the future queen Catherine Howard also visited the site in 1541. Most notably, Catherine of Aragon spent time at Buckden during her enforced separation from court before being transferred to Kimbolton Castle. As a result, the village became part of the chain of locations associated with one of the defining royal disputes in English history. Its surviving medieval towers provide a tangible reminder of the Tudor figures who once passed through its gates. St Ives owes much of its historic importance to King John. In 1001, the remains of St Ivo were reportedly discovered nearby, helping establish the town as an important religious centre. By the early 13th century, King John had granted St Ives one of England’s most significant fairs, transforming its fortunes and helping it develop into a thriving market town. Royal patronage brought merchants from across the country and elevated St Ives’ regional importance. While visitors today know the town for its picturesque bridge and riverside setting, its growth was closely tied to medieval royal influence. Wisbech has a lesser-known royal story linked to the turbulence of the 17th century. During the English Civil War and the years that followed, the Fens became a region of strategic importance. Local tradition and historical accounts connect the town with Charles II who renewed and enlarged Wisbech's Carter of Incorporation in 1669. Wisbech Castle itself has hosted numerous notable figures through the centuries and stands as a reminder of the town’s longstanding relationship with authority and power. metadata.title: Cambs woman, 87, scammed out of £7,000 as police launch investigation
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire Constabulary have launched an investigation after an 87-year-old woman was scammed out of £7,000 in a courier fraud scheme.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs woman, 87, scammed out of £7,000 as police launch investigation
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have launched an investigation after an 87-year-old woman was scammed out of £7,000 in a courier fraud scheme. The Peterborough woman received a landline call on October 12 from a man claiming to be a Cambridgeshire police officer. He told her that a man had been arrested for theft and found with counterfeit money, and that £7,000 had been taken from her account but later returned. The caller said they needed her help to investigate and told her to stay on the line while he connected her to her bank. After a brief dial tone, the woman was put through to a female caller who claimed to be from the bank and confirmed the officer’s story. The fraudster told her to withdraw £7,000 for the investigation and keep the reason from bank staff. She was told to take the money home, where someone would collect it using the code word "orange 123." A man later arrived at her door, gave the code word, and took the envelope of cash. The woman later realised she had been scammed and the money was gone. A police investigation was launched, which the force confirmed on October 21 is still ongoing. In a statement to social media, Cambridgeshire Police said: "Sadly, our officers are seeing more and more of these cases of courier fraud scams and they are urging people to be vigilant and look out for vulnerable neighbours and relatives. "Remember, neither the police nor your bank will ever call and ask you to withdraw money as part of an investigation. "If in doubt, hang up and call police on 101 from another line to check before you act." More information on fraud prevention is available on the Cambridgeshire Police website.

metadata.title: Popular discount retailer could be coming to town under new plans
metadata.contentSnippet: Popular discount retailer Home Bargains could be opening a store in Huntingdon under fresh plans.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Popular discount retailer could be coming to town under new plans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A popular discount retailer with sites across the UK could be opening a store in Huntingdon under fresh plans. Applicant TG Morris Limited, which trades as Home Bargains, has lodged plans for a new retail unit on St Peters Road. If approved, the "comprehensive development" would also provide customer and service access, car parking and landscaping. The site is surrounded by retail and commercial buildings, including Bensons for Beds and Wickes retail stores to the north. It is currently an "undeveloped plot" presenting an "opportunity to deliver a planned commercial scheme," a design and access statement said. According to the plans, the "high-quality" development would re-purpose the site, providing local people "with choice and quality of provision". Applicant TG Morris has lodged plans for a new retail unit on St Peter's Road (Image: WPL Consulting) The proposed development would also create new full and part-time jobs while creating an "attractive and welcoming environment". Comprising more 24,500 square feet, the store would feature an additional 7,500 square-foot garden centre. It would feature composite cladding at the upper level with brick work below and glazed shopfronts in keeping with the retailer's branding. Spread across one storey, the store would "reutilise and modify an existing access point from St Peters Road. A planning and retail statement submitted as part of the application highlighted Home Bargains' "aggressive expansion strategy". Documents outlining the chain's retail requirements for 2024-25 said its ongoing success was "built on the offer of top brands at bottom prices". The proposed development would "deliver a number of significant benefits to the local economy", the plans added. This includes "supporting the vitality and viability of the local retail offer" and "enhancement of retail choice and qualitative retail offer". "The development represents a substantial investment in Huntingdon that will ensure the delivery of a high-quality and modern retail building and wider site improvements. "The proposals will also secure the long-term occupation of the site, create new jobs and will result in significant investment both directly and indirectly in the local economy." metadata.title: Hinchingbrooke hospital garden becomes living tribute to respected horticulturist
metadata.contentSnippet: A hospital garden in Huntingdon is blooming into a living tribute to a lifelong horticulturist David White.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hinchingbrooke hospital garden becomes living tribute to respected horticulturist
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A hospital garden in Huntingdon is blooming into a living tribute to a lifelong horticulturist. David White, a former president of Anglia in Bloom and a respected plantsman, died last month at Hinchingbrooke Hospital. Now, his daughter Carley and granddaughter Kaia—who both work at the hospital—are continuing his legacy by championing the Education Centre Garden, a space he cherished deeply. Carley White, team leader for Hinchingbrooke Community Midwives, said: "Dad's association with the garden spans over many years. Tribute to volunteer gardener (Image: Hinchingbrooke Hospital) "I spent two long stints in hospital as a teenager, and he would push me in my bed down to the garden every day. "More recently we spent many hours in the garden in the weeks before he sadly passed." The garden is supported by a dedicated team of hospital volunteers and was recognised last year with a Royal Horticultural Society Outstanding Award for 'Gardening for Health and Wellbeing'—an honour it received thanks to a nomination from Mr White. Kaia White, a paediatrics medical secretary, said: "Grandpa loved the Hinchingbrooke garden, and the volunteers do such a fantastic job. Certificate for RHS (Image: Hinchingbrooke Hospital) "It held a very special place in his heart—as it does in mine and Mum's." The family has donated plants from Mr White's nursery to the hospital garden and other community green spaces. Kaia added: "It's lovely to be able to give back to Hinchingbrooke Hospital when it has given so much to us." David White (Image: Hinchingbrooke Hospital) Mr White’s horticultural career included work at Kew Gardens and Buckingham Palace. He also contributed to planting schemes along major road networks during his time with the Department of Transport. His family hopes the garden will continue to serve as a place of peace and healing for patients, staff, and visitors—a lasting reminder of his passion for horticulture and community.

metadata.title: Hinchingbrooke English department shortlisted for national teaching award
metadata.contentSnippet: The English department at Hinchingbrooke School in Huntingdon has been shortlisted for a national education award.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hinchingbrooke English department shortlisted for national teaching award
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Hinchingbrooke School’s English department has been shortlisted for a national education award. The team in Huntingdon is in the running for The PTI’s Bernice McCabe Award, which celebrates excellence in subject leadership and teaching. The PTI, formerly known as the Prince’s Teaching Institute, is a national education charity that supports teachers and school leaders through high-quality professional development. Dr Cat Scutt MBE, chief executive of The PTI, said: "The Bernice McCabe Award celebrates the exceptional teachers and departments who demonstrate the transformative power of great subject teaching. "Their expertise, dedication and passion for their subjects can inspire young people, deepen their understanding and open up new possibilities for their future. "We are delighted to recognise this year’s shortlisted departments and to celebrate the teachers whose commitment to their subjects and their students makes such a lasting difference." Named in memory of Bernice McCabe OBE, the founding co-director of The PTI who died in February 2019, the award honours departments that put inspiring subject teaching at the heart of the classroom. The winning department will receive a £5,000 prize and a trophy. Hinchingbrooke’s English department is one of three nominees for the 2026 award, alongside the PE department at Priory School in Lewes and the English department at Thomas Tallis School in Greenwich. The PTI promotes subject-centred teaching as a sustainable approach to school improvement, helping teachers deepen their expertise and share a love of learning with students. Significant funding from Postcode Lottery players has enabled The PTI to support both nominated and winning schools, giving them the resources and skills needed to deliver outstanding lessons. Since 2018, players have raised more than £1.5 million for The PTI, impacting the educational experiences of hundreds of thousands of young people across England and Wales.

metadata.title: WATCH: The Cambridgeshire fire station trying to 'break the taboo of menopause'
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service is trying to "break the taboo of menopause" by educating firefighters about women's health.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: The Cambridgeshire fire station trying to 'break the taboo of menopause'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire fire station is trying to "break the taboo of menopause" by educating firefighters about women's health. Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson visited Huntingdon Fire and Rescue Station on October 15 to mark Menopause Awareness Month. Ms Phillipson said there was still “quite a lot of ignorance” about the menopause and its effects on women, especially at work. She said: "We know that there is still far too much stigma around this and it's good we are speaking more about the health challenges and women's experiences around the menopause. "Employers leading the way are providing a culture where people can be open about the things they might be experiencing and the impact the menopause can have. "One example we have talked about here is just making sure we have period products available routinely for firefighters who might be out on jobs and can't get back to the site to get what they need." Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson Government figures show that only about one in 10 firefighters nationally are women, far fewer than in the police force. At Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service, women make up 24 per cent of firefighters, with about a third aged 40 to 55. Huntingdon Fire Station’s menopause champion Hayley Douglas said supporting women through health challenges could help increase those numbers. Hayley said: "We're doing an awful lot as a sector to try and encourage more women to join the fire and rescue service and I think this is a really important part of that. Menopause Champion Hayley Douglas "Firefighting is a career, so people join in their early twenties for example. "We need to make sure we support them through their life cycle of hormones as well." Huntingdon Fire Station has put period protection packs in every toilet and fire engine, as well as portable toilets and tents on its engines. Huntingdon Fire Station has introduced period protection items in every fire engine The station also delivers mandatory training to everyone in the organisation about the symptoms of the menopause, how it impacts work and its effects on relationships. Hayley said: "We are a male majority organisation and a lot of the engagement during those sessions has been from our male colleagues, understanding what their partners at home are going through. "Increasing that knowledge at work is like throwing a stone and seeing all the rippled effect where people start talking about it outside of work as well. "In the service, it's given women the confidence to be able to go and speak to their line manager knowing they have had a level of input in menopause awareness. "It just makes it easier to have that conversation. "Ultimately what we are trying to do is break the taboo of menopause and make people feel like it is a safe environment to openly talk about what they are going through." October marks Menopause Awareness Month Ms Phillipson added: "Often, quite small practical changes around uniform and kit and making sure you have good toilet facilities can just make the world of difference. "From next spring, bigger employers will have to publish plans on how they are taking action to support women including in areas like the menopause. "But already we have employers like Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service who are showing what can be done." Employers with 250 or more staff can currently publish a voluntary action plan on their gender pay gap and support for employees experiencing the menopause. Subject to legislation, the plans will become mandatory from spring 2027.

metadata.title: Everything we know so far after fire at proposed asylum seeker site
metadata.contentSnippet: Emergency services have descended on Roman Court, Leverington, near Wisbech after a single-storey building fire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Everything we know so far after fire at proposed asylum seeker site
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Emergency services have descended on a site earmarked for asylum seeker accommodation in Cambridgeshire. Here's everything we know so far. Firefighters were called to the blaze at Roman Court, Leverington, near Wisbech, at 7.26pm on Wednesday (October 21). Crews from Wisbech, March and Dogsthorpe, along with the turntable ladder from Stanground rushed to the scene. Appliances from Outwell and West Walton, in Norfolk, also attended the incident, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service confirmed. A spokesperson said: "Firefighters arrived to find a fire in a single storey building that was unoccupied. "They are working hard to tackle the fire and prevent it from spreading. There are currently no injuries reported. "An investigation will be carried out to establish the cause of the fire once it is fully extinguished." Roman Court has been at the centre of an asylum row since the government announced plans to house 26 mothers and babies at the site. In September, Fenland District Council revealed it had been told by the Home Office the site could "provide 26 bed spaces for mothers and babies". The proposal forms part of a national move from hotels into longer-term accommodation. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: ‘Extreme danger’ posed by modified e-bikes as faulty battery implicated in fatal fire
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire County Council is warning of the “extreme risk” posed by illegally modified e-bikes after a faulty battery was implicated in the deaths of two children.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: ‘Extreme danger’ posed by modified e-bikes as faulty battery implicated in fatal fire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire County Council is warning of the “extreme risk” posed by illegally modified e-bikes after a faulty battery was implicated in the deaths of two children. An ongoing inquest into the fire which claimed the lives of Gemma Germeney, 31, and her two children, aged eight and four, heard the “most probable” cause of the fire was the “failure of a charging battery pack”. Cambridgeshire County Council backed a motion calling for better awareness of the rules around e-bikes and e-scooters as modified vehicles can pose “extreme danger to the public”. Cllr Anna Bradnam, of Waterbeach, said the inquest had found that the battery had been replaced and “wired in a way that made it dangerous”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “I think we owe it to our residents to make it absolutely abundantly clear what risks they’re taking if they choose to alter the batteries. “This is not just for the people who buy them, it’s for the people working in garages who might be asked to solve an electrical problem. “Having these batteries that are very powerful and being charged in homes overnight is an extreme risk and I wouldn’t want it to happen to anybody else.” Cllr David Levien, of Trumpington, who brought forward the motion, said that modified vehicles can cause serious injuries through not just speed – but their weight too. The Lib Dem councillor said: “The high-performance models are heavy and at their top legal speed contain sufficient energy to be capable of causing serious injury or death to members of the public as well as the rider. I have seen, and no doubt others here will have seen, e-bikes being ridden in public at speeds greater than 40 miles per hour – some are even capable of 70 miles per hour.” Under current laws, e-bikes have a capped speed of 15.5mph and cannot have a maximum motor power of more than 250W – but conversion kits can be bought to change this. E-scooters are always illegal on public land unless rented from a company like Voi. The Lib Dem councillor also requested more data from hospitals on injuries and deaths so the “true nature of the danger of these vehicles can be better understood”. Cllr Geoffrey Seeff, of St Neots The Eatons, said a BBC report in 2025 found a London hospital had dealt with 150 serious injuries in six months involving both children and adults. The Lib Dem councillor said: “Because of their motors and batteries, these machines are extremely heavy and cause horrific damage in a collision or if they fall on the rider. “Numerous deaths have been reported both here and in the USA, we have tried unsuccessfully thus far to obtain the relevant statistics for Cambridgeshire and the country as a whole.” Cllr Christopher Morris, chair of the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Fire Authority, said that the vehicles are a “transformative technology”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “Regulating transformative technology is always a balancing act – we must support rapid adoption while making sure it does not run ahead of sensible risk management. “Our fire service recognises the growing risks linked to e-bike lithium ion batteries and that around three quarters of identifiable e-bike fires involve conversion kits, mismatched chargers or other post-purchase modifications. “I support this motion and the members’ bill that it references and additionally I would urge everyone involved to keep fire risk firmly in view at every stage.”

metadata.title: RSPCA issues urgent plea as 61 multi-animal cases hit Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: The RSPCA in Cambridgeshire is overwhelmed with "multi-animal cases" and has issued an urgent plea for help.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: RSPCA issues urgent plea as 61 multi-animal cases hit Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The RSPCA in Cambridgeshire is overwhelmed with "multi-animal cases" and has issued an urgent plea for help. The charity is appealing for "extra-special adopters" as rescue teams struggle with rising cases of animals, sometimes more than 100, being housed at single addresses. So far this year, RSPCA frontline officers are dealing with an average 410 "multi-animal" incidents - involving 10 or more every single month - an increase on 2025 which was a record-breaking year. Ronnie, Cane corso crossbreed, aged one (Image: RSPCA) Across Cambridgeshire, there have already been a staggering 61 incidents between January and August. Many of the animals rescued from these homes have behavioural and medical needs requiring rehabilitation. Currently, at the RSPCA Block Fen Animal Centre, cats Arthur and Tizzy are looking for their forever homes, having previously lived in a multi-cat household. Dogs Ronnie, Lulu and Marlon and Posy are also waiting for adopters this Adoptober. Jo Rowland, chief executive for the RSPCA, said: "We are struggling and we urgently need help. "Our frontline officers are finding dozens, even hundreds of animals in need at single addresses. "Animals who have come from homes like this often have behavioural and medical needs, due to the environment they had been living in and need a little more care and understanding. Lulu, Shar-Pei, aged six (Image: RSPCA) "We need to get pets out of our centres and into loving homes so we can continue to rescue." The charity said rising levels of multi-animal cases are putting unprecedented pressure on its teams and volunteers across England and Wales - with 3,280 multi-animal cases reported across England and Wales already this year - an average of 410 incidents each month. Arthur, domestic shorthair, aged one (Image: RSPCA) Last year, RSPCA frontline officers responded to more than 4,200 incidents involving 10 or more animals at a single address. These incidents involved 88,000 animals including dogs, cats, small pets, horses and exotic animals, and 75 of those cases involved more than 100 animals - more than one every single week. For more information on how to help, visit the RSPCA website.

metadata.title: Putting the focus on East Anglia’s community changemakers
metadata.contentSnippet: Enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027 by November 8. Celebrate energy innovation, community sustainability and regional environmental champions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Putting the focus on East Anglia’s community changemakers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: There are just a few weeks remaining to submit your entries for the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027 and be in with a chance of being recognised as one of the region’s sustainability champions. Bringing together the ambitions of Insight Energy magazine and the Clean & Green campaign, these awards were created to put the spotlight on businesses, organisations and individuals who are making a difference, whether through innovation, education, green energy or environmentally friendly business practices. The entry deadline is Sunday, November 8, after which time the judging process will begin and 2027’s finalists will be shortlisted. Read on to find out more about two of the 14 categories. Sponsored by National Grid The Energy Innovation Award will recognise innovations that significantly enhance energy efficiency or reduce energy consumption. From businesses to local communities, there are countless people actively looking at their green credentials, and this award will celebrate those who are meeting their environmental commitments in a way that hasn’t been seen before. The category is open to any individual or organisation that can showcase an energy innovation that is both unique and groundbreaking. The judges will be looking for entries that demonstrate a novel and scalable approach with measurable results in reducing environmental impact, while actively engaging key stakeholders. Entrants will be expected to demonstrate how their innovation can be scaled or applied across other industries or regions, thereby maximising its impact. They will also need to show how they have actively involved energy providers, consumers or other stakeholders in their innovation. Critically, anyone entering this category must be able to evidence a reduction in energy consumption or improved energy efficiency, demonstrating measurable outcomes. An individual, group or organisation that has gone above and beyond to drive sustainability within their local community will be named Community Champion of the Year. This award recognises local heroes who have demonstrated outstanding leadership, innovation and commitment to creating meaningful environmental change while inspiring others to take action. The judges will be looking for entrants who can show a clear and positive impact on their community, whether through grassroots initiatives, community projects, education programmes, or other innovative means. Entries should provide evidence of measurable outcomes wherever possible, highlighting the real-world impact of the entrant’s work and the creative or unique approaches they have used to address environmental challenges. A key aspect of this award is the ability to engage and collaborate with others. Entrants should demonstrate how they have brought people together, encouraging participation and fostering a shared commitment to improving sustainability at a local level. If you think you or someone you know has made a lasting impact on the future of your community, now is the time to enter. Find out more about all the categories and enter at cleanandgreenawards.co.uk

metadata.contentSnippet: Children’s gymnastics coach Aaron Strachan, from Huntingdon, has been jailed after he was found with more than 17,000 indecent images of children.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Gymnastics coach found with over 17,000 indecent images of children pictured
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A children’s gymnastics coach from Cambridgeshire who was found with more than 17,000 indecent images of children has been jailed. Aaron Strachan was arrested on suspicion of making indecent images of children in August 2024. Police received information that he could have indecent material on his phone. Officers found a total of 17,147 indecent images of children on the phone, mainly of young or pre-pubescent boys. These included 6,080 category C images, 6,028 category B images and 5,039 category A images – the most severe. Also found on the phone were 56 group chats from a messaging app where indecent images were requested and shared, including by Strachan. In interview, Strachan, of Robertson Way, Sapley, Huntingdon, denied any knowledge of the indecent images found on his phone. He claimed he had no idea how the material may have got there. The 26-year-old then suggested he may have left his phone unlocked and that someone else could have accessed it at work. This was despite evidence that the images were downloaded, viewed and shared at various times of the day and night over several months. However, on the day his trial was due to begin, Strachan pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of children. He also admitted one count of distributing an indecent image or video. Detective Constable Matthew Walshe, who investigated, said: "Strachan was found with many indecent images of pre-pubescent boys, while working as a gymnastics coach teaching boys of a similar age. "While none of the children in the indecent images on Strachan’s phone have been found to be children he knew or worked with, every one of those 17,147 images represents a child who was sexually abused or exploited. "Strachan’s own safeguarding training will have taught him the horrific consequences such abuse carries for every child. "Despite the weight of evidence and knowledge of his guilt, he pleaded not guilty to delay justice as long as possible before changing his plea at the beginning of the trial. "He is a committed paedophile who is now facing the consequences of his actions, which includes never working with children again." Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: BBC to axe 3 major channels in huge shake-up as broadcaster makes £500m cuts
metadata.contentSnippet: BBC to close BBC Three, Radio 4 Extra and BBC Scotland in spring 2027, moving content online while seeking £500m in savings.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: BBC to axe 3 major channels in huge shake-up as broadcaster makes £500m cuts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The BBC is set to close three of its broadcast channels as part of cost-cutting plans to save £500 million by 2028. BBC Three, Radio 4 Extra, and the BBC Scotland channel will all go off air in spring 2027. The move is part of wider financial pressures facing the broadcaster, with content from the affected channels to remain available through digital platforms. BBC Director-General Matt Brittin said: "We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. "We all know that means tough choices. "Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy it on iPlayer and Sounds. "While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues." BBC Three content, which has a younger-skewing audience, will be available on BBC iPlayer and on other platforms, including YouTube. It is not the first time BBC Three has been cut from linear TV. It returned as a fully-fledged TV channel in January 2022, six years after it moved online. The channel has since been responsible for major hits including Fleabag, Normal People and Killing Eve. Programmes from Radio 4 Extra will still be available on BBC Sounds – and The Daily Service will be on BBC Sounds and local radio. 🎣 Gone Fishing returns Sunday 25 October Two friends, beautiful places and a good natter. Join Mortimer and Whitehouse for a new series and one last fish with Ted More ➡️ https://t.co/7dx30HJakU https://t.co/8R0JzH3a27 — BBC Press Office (@bbcpress) October 20, 2026 BBC Scotland will remain available on iPlayer, with content also shown on BBC One and BBC Two in Scotland. In addition, around 100 jobs will be cut at BBC News, as the corporation faces pressure to make savings of £500 million by 2028. A number of roles will also be cut as a result of the broadcast closures, including ten in Scotland. Today’s announcement follows earlier savings revealed in BBC Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, and other divisions. Further changes are expected, with new Director of BBC News Rachel Jupp set to outline additional savings plans early next year. At the weekend the BBC confirmed its long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be “rested” next year amid the corporation’s ongoing “savings challenges”. Will you miss BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Waterbeach heritage walk reveals how history is shaping the new town
metadata.contentSnippet: A heritage walk has brought the history of Waterbeach to life, highlighting how the past is influencing its future development.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Waterbeach heritage walk reveals how history is shaping the new town
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A heritage walk has brought the history of Waterbeach to life, highlighting how the past is influencing its future development. Last weekend, more than 55 people took part in the guided walk, which explored the village’s historical sites and showed how they are shaping the design and character of the new town. The route included access to areas not currently accessible to the public, which will be opened up to recreate the historic Causeway connection between Waterbeach Abbey and Denny Abbey. Jane Williamson, chair of trustees at The Farmland Museum, said: "The Heritage Walk was a wonderful community event, and I saw people I haven’t seen for ages and met some new ones too. "There’s was something really moving about going through the gate into the bit of causeway that has been inaccessible for so long. The walk explored Waterbeach’s history and its developing new town (Image: Waterbeach) "The walk along the path from the new town towards the Abbey is absolutely lovely, it’s almost like being in another world." The walk began at Waterbeach Village Green and included a visit to the Waterbeach Military Heritage Museum. It continued through Soldiers Hill, an ancient earthwork, and included a visit to Denny Abbey. Along the route, participants heard from historians and community leaders who explained how the new development is incorporating historical features into its design, including street names and transport links. Reverend Sarah Newns, pioneer minister at St John’s Church, said: "The walk showed the importance of connecting with neighbours and sharing experiences whether you have lived here a long time or are new to the area. "The history of the land is fascinating, and this walk alone showed the layers of history around us, as well as how the next chapter of the parish is being written and shaped by the new development." To find out more about Waterbeach’s heritage, visit waterbeachwb.co.uk/heritage.

metadata.title: Councillors vote to refuse controversial 199-home Ramsey plan
metadata.contentSnippet: HDC councillors have voted to refuse a controversial 199-home development plan for Ramsey despite receiving a recommendation for approval.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Councillors vote to refuse controversial 199-home Ramsey plan
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Councillors have voted to refuse a controversial 199-home development plan for Ramsey despite receiving a recommendation for approval. BDW Trading Ltd submitted the proposal for land south of The Malting with landowners Susan and Robert Pickard. The scheme included up to 199 homes, 40 per cent affordable housing, children’s play areas, drainage infrastructure and related works. Developers also proposed a landscaped perimeter, a 1.1km circular walking route linked to public rights of way and green infrastructure covering around 37 per cent of the site. The site is land south of The Malting in Ramsey However, at a meeting on October 19, Huntingdonshire District Council's Development Management Committee voted to refuse the outline application, which had been recommended for approval. Planning officers said the benefits outweighed the harm, pointing to Huntingdonshire’s current shortfall in five-year housing land supply. The report said the scheme would help meet housing need and provide substantial affordable housing. Cllr Andrew Wood proposed refusing the plan against officers’ recommendation, subject to consultation with the Secretary of State. The proposal passed with nine votes in favour, none against and two abstentions. The decision followed strong opposition from residents, who submitted 228 objection letters, as well as from Ramsey Town Council, Bury Parish Council and the Middle Level Commissioners. Residents warned of more traffic, pressure on schools and healthcare services, flood risk, countryside loss, damage to wildlife and further merging of Ramsey and Bury. Ramsey Town Council said the application conflicted with the emerging Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan, which seeks to keep Ramsey and Bury separate. Sam Carling, MP for North West Cambridgeshire, told the council the development would pile more pressure on the area’s already struggling Integrated Care Board. Sam Carling, MP for North West Cambridgeshire A formal decision notice on the plan has not yet been issued by the Local Planning Authority.

metadata.title: 10 pumpkin picking spots in Cambridgeshire for Halloween
metadata.contentSnippet: Discover Cambridgeshire pumpkin patches and Halloween attractions, from maize mazes and spooky trails to family fun at Milton Maze, Wimpole Estate and more.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 pumpkin picking spots in Cambridgeshire for Halloween
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families across Cambridgeshire are heading out to find the perfect pumpkin as Halloween approaches, with giant pumpkin fields, maize mazes, spooky trails and family-friendly autumn attractions to choose from. Here are 10 of the best in the local area: Johnsons of Old Hurst is hosting a Halloween event with no booking required, allowing visitors to pay at the zoo gate on arrival and enjoy a Halloween Magic Show, special guests, tea and cakes in the Tea Room, and a free children’s treasure trail suitable for all ages and families. Skylark’s annual “Week of Wickedness” is one of Fenland’s biggest Halloween attractions, offering pumpkin picking, a spooky maize maze, tractor rides and family-friendly entertainment. Milton Maze, one of the best-known pumpkin patches near Cambridge, has tens of thousands of pumpkins, Halloween shows, food stalls and its popular Field of Fun. Rusty’s Great Pumpkin Patch at Worzals has more than 80,000 pumpkins, themed areas, family games and seasonal food, with every ticket including a pumpkin to take home and much of the attraction undercover. A favourite among families from Peterborough and north Cambridgeshire, Sacrewell's Pumpkin Festival combines pumpkin picking with Halloween trails, animal encounters and plenty of autumn-themed entertainment. The National Trust estate is a popular autumn destination, with seasonal family activities, harvest displays and pumpkin-themed events during October. Its picturesque parkland provides the perfect backdrop for an autumn day out. Cuckoo Bridge Farm offers a pick-your-own patch, with other attractions that include a straw maze, spooky graveyard, bouncy castle and children’s play area. Freshfields offers free entry and lets visitors pick sunflowers, potatoes and sweetcorn. Lincoln Farm opens this weekend (18/19), then from October 25 to 30, with goats, and fluffy chicks. The garden centre is free to enter, has more than 500 pumpkins and includes a new spooky maze this year.

metadata.title: 9 buildings in Cambridgeshire hiding centuries of history
metadata.contentSnippet: From Roman burial monuments and medieval churches to grand Jacobean mansions, Cambridgeshire is home to some extraordinary historic buildings.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 9 buildings in Cambridgeshire hiding centuries of history
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From Roman burial monuments and medieval churches to grand Jacobean mansions, Cambridgeshire is home to some extraordinary historic buildings. These nine landmarks have witnessed centuries of change and continue to tell the story of the county's rich and fascinating past. Few buildings in Cambridgeshire can match the historical weight of Peterborough Cathedral. The site has been a place of worship since the 7th century, when an Anglo-Saxon monastery was founded here in 655AD. Over the centuries it grew into one of England's most important medieval abbeys and later became the striking Norman cathedral seen today. The cathedral is famous as the burial place of Katherine of Aragon, Henry VIII's first wife. Mary Queen of Scots was also buried here before her remains were moved to Westminster Abbey. Viking raids, the Dissolution of the Monasteries and the English Civil War all left their mark on the building, making it a living record of England's turbulent past. Tucked away in a suburban corner of Peterborough, Longthorpe Tower looks modest from the outside but hides one of Britain's greatest medieval treasures. Built between about 1290 and 1300 by lawyer Robert Thorpe as part of a manor house, the tower contains an collection of wall paintings dating from around 1330. These rare artworks survived because they were covered with whitewash after the Reformation and remained hidden until the 20th century. The paintings depict religious scenes, morality tales, animals, kings and everyday medieval life. Buckden Towers has witnessed nearly 900 years of history in the heart of Huntingdonshire. Originally established as a residence for the Bishops of Lincoln during the 12th century, the fortified palace became one of the most important ecclesiastical residences in England. Numerous monarchs stayed here, including Henry III, Edward I and Richard III. Perhaps its most famous resident was Katherine of Aragon, who was confined here in 1533 during Henry VIII's attempts to end their marriage. The surviving brick tower, gatehouse and moated grounds evoke both the medieval and Tudor periods. Located in the former grammar school attended by Oliver Cromwell, this building offers a direct link to one of the most controversial figures in British history. The medieval structure dates back centuries and was already well established when a young Cromwell studied there in the late 16th century. The school would have provided him with a classical education that helped shape the future Lord Protector. Over the years the building has served many different purposes, but its strongest association remains with the man who led Parliament's forces during the English Civil War. Known as the "Ship of the Fens", Ely Cathedral dominates the landscape for miles around. Construction began in 1083 after the Norman Conquest, although the site had religious significance long before that. The cathedral is renowned for its magnificent Octagon Tower, created after the original Norman crossing tower collapsed in 1322. Its architecture reflects centuries of development, from Norman stonework to Gothic grandeur. Throughout its history it has survived political upheaval, religious reform and civil conflict. Just a short walk from Ely Cathedral stands the only surviving residence of Oliver Cromwell apart from Hampton Court. Parts of the building date back to around 1215, making it one of Ely's oldest houses. Originally serving as the vicarage for nearby St Mary's Church, it became home to Cromwell and his family between 1636 and 1647. From here he managed church tithes and lived during the years leading up to the English Civil War. The timber-framed building has survived centuries of change and now operates as a museum. Behind an elegant Georgian façade in Wisbech lies a building filled with stories of wealth, philanthropy and local influence. Built in 1722, Peckover House became home to the prominent Quaker banking family whose name still resonates in Fenland history. The family used their success to support a wide range of charitable projects throughout the region. Today managed by the National Trust, the house contains richly decorated interiors that contrast with its plain exterior. The surrounding walled garden is equally remarkable, featuring rare plants, historic structures and even orange trees believed to be centuries old. This handsome Georgian townhouse on Wisbech's South Brink was built around 1740 but is best known as the birthplace of social reformer Octavia Hill in 1838. Hill later became one of the founders of the National Trust and transformed housing conditions for some of London's poorest residents. The house was home to her family during formative years in her life and reflects the prosperity of one of Wisbech's leading merchant families. Saved and restored by volunteers, the building now tells the story not only of Hill's achievements but also of the social history of Victorian Britain. Just west of Peterborough, Elton Hall has been continuously occupied by the same family for generations. Parts of the building date to the 15th century, while later additions introduced Tudor and Gothic influences. The hall has welcomed royalty, survived political upheavals and accumulated centuries of family stories. Its striking architecture reflects changing fashions across hundreds of years, creating a building that feels like a timeline of English country-house history. Surrounded by landscaped parkland, Elton Hall remains privately owned and still contains family treasures that connect modern visitors directly with the past. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Cromwell Museum unveils rare artefacts in ‘A Few of Our Favourite Things’ exhibition
metadata.contentSnippet: A new exhibition is being held at the Cromwell Museum in Huntingdon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cromwell Museum unveils rare artefacts in ‘A Few of Our Favourite Things’ exhibition
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new exhibition is being held at the Cromwell Museum in Huntingdon. Titled 'A Few of Our Favourite Things', the exhibition will be showcasing selected items by the museum’s volunteers, staff, and trustees. The exhibition offers a personal glimpse into the artefacts that resonate most with those closely involved with the collection. This includes items from the museum’s stores that are not typically displayed. The museum is housed in the former grammar school where Oliver Cromwell was educated. It holds a collection of objects that relate to his life and times. Cromwell Museum 2026 exterior (Image: Cromwell Museum) Among the chosen pieces are weapons, documents, portraits, and diplomatic gifts, each revealing different aspects of Cromwell’s legacy. The exhibition will run until November 1. One of the highlights of the exhibition is the Christmas Ban Proclamation of 1647. This ordinance by Parliament attempted to suppress Christmas, Easter, and other festivities, leading to riots and widespread resistance. Although often associated with Cromwell, historical records indicate he had little direct involvement with the ban. Another notable artefact is Cromwell’s 'Mortuary' Cavalry Sword circa 1650. The finely balanced weapon is believed to have been passed down through his family and still bears the initials 'OC' on the blade. The sword shows signs of use, serving as a reminder of the close-contact combat during the Civil War. Also on display is Cromwell’s Letter of 1652, offering a rare glimpse of the private man behind the public figure. Model of the Naseby Ship (Image: The Cromwell Museum) Other exhibition highlights include original copies of the Instrument of Government and the Humble Petition and Advice, the constitutional documents that shaped the Protectorate. A unique favourite is the working model of the Naseby, Cromwell’s flagship of 1655, built by master modelmaker Fred Pearl. The museum is open from Tuesday to Sunday, 10am to 4pm. The exhibition is free to visit, with donations welcomed.

metadata.title: Community primary school 'coming out the other side' after devastating fire
metadata.contentSnippet: Fen Drayton Primary School is finally returning to normal life after a devastating fire forced staff and pupils out of the building for a year.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Community primary school 'coming out the other side' after devastating fire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire primary school is "coming out the other side" and finally returning to normal life after a devastating fire forced staff and pupils out of the building for a year. Fen Drayton Primary School, which has 82 pupils, was badly damaged by a fire on August 13, 2024, that started accidentally during roof work. More than 30 firefighters tackled the blaze while an ambulance and three Hazardous Area Response Team vehicles were dispatched to treat a man for "serious burns". The blaze ripped through the school's ceilings, made the school unusable and forced pupils into mobile classrooms on the playing field. The damage left the building unusable A week later, heavy storms caused further water damage because the roof was not yet watertight. Nina McQueen, who has been headteacher for six years, said: "It was the year five and six classroom that was damaged the most. "The teacher had been in a couple of days before and set her classroom up ready for September. "She had got all the stationery out and labelled all the books and everything. The blaze ripped through the school's ceilings The fire in August 2024 caused devastating damage to Fen Drayton Primary School "Everything in her room had to be disposed of, because the fire was over the corner of her room, so she lost everything: books, tables, chairs, everything that was in her room. "I think that was really hard for her." Ms McQueen said the small staff team pulled together to cope with the devastation. Headteacher Nina McQueen She said: "It was obviously very challenging; we were very upset at the time, particularly when we came in and saw the devastation in the building. The headteacher's office was damaged "There were lots of tears from staff, particularly those who were affected the most by the damage and lost personal items from their classrooms. "But everyone pulled together and everyone was really supportive - and I think the same with the children." The school stayed closed for several weeks in September 2024 while two mobile classrooms were installed on the field. All 82 pupils were taught there for a year while the school was renovated. Pupils had to learn in mobile buildings on the school field for a year Ms McQueen said she worried about how pupils would cope, but they took the disruption in their stride. Insurance did not cover all the repair costs, so local groups donated up to £2,000 to replace lost resources and support pupils during the disruption. The PTA arranged special experiences and days out for pupils during the disruption. Parents and the parish council also helped, while the village hall housed pupils before the mobile classrooms were ready. Staff and pupils returned to the renovated building in September last year, and a new extension to the school's reception area was officially opened on October 10. The pupils and staff have now returned to the newly renovated school building The school building is now usable again (Image: Newsquest) Ms McQueen said she feels that life at the school is beginning to return to normal. She said: "We are coming out the other side of it. "Last year was quite challenging, getting back in the building, moving everything back in, getting everything set up and trying to get back to normal. "But I would say that we are definitely there now." Ms McQueen said she believes the incident shows the sense of community at the school Ms McQueen said she believes that the impact of the fire showed what a strong community there is at Fen Drayton Primary School. She added: "I think we can get through anything."
