summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire County Council has been ranked among the worst in the country for providing care plans for children with special needs within the deadline. A Freedom of Information request showed that the council is facing an active backlog of around 1,800 cases. Children who are referred for an education, health and care plan (EHCP) should receive one within 20 weeks – but last year, less than one in ten were provided within the deadline. In the 2025/26 financial year, 93.33 per cent of EHCPs were issued after the deadline – with some children facing long waits. Cambridgeshire ranked 142nd out of 148 local authorities which reported their figures nationwide. Labour councillors Alex Bulat and Bryony Goodliffe submitted the original FOI request and put the figures to Cambridgeshire County Council calling for a review. Cllr Bulat, of St Ives South and Needingworth, said: “The reality on the ground is that people don’t care about excuses. Our residents don’t care about blaming others because our case workers are being asked to manage up to 500 cases each – two and a half the regional average – and parents and children are left waiting.” Cllr Elliot Tong said he had asked the council for the longest wait time and was told this was 150 weeks – nearly three years. The independent councillor, of Abbey, said: “These are real children whose lives are affected by our choices and the fact that a child has had to wait three years to get the support that they are entitled to is absolutely abhorrent.” Council leader Lucy Nethsingha amended the motion and removed any references to the FOI figures leading to accusations of politicising it by opposition members. “Conservative group leader Ross Martin said the Liberal Democrats were “trying to blame everyone but themselves”. He said: “You’re playing politics with our children – we want to get on with delivering for them because my inbox is full of issues with ECHPs, as it is in my day job as well. This isn’t acceptable – it’s more than just the 20 week delays, it’s the delays in the refreshers. “There’s an example I’m aware of in Godmanchester where someone has been waiting for five years for an update – that’s not acceptable.” Cllr Edna Murphy, chair of the children and young people committee, agreed that wait times “aren’t where they should be” but assured councillors fixing it “is a top priority”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “We haven’t been doing nothing, we have been working incredibly hard on this for just over a year since we took control. “Although there is a lot more to do there has been significant improvement in the service in that time. “In just over a year the council is now producing three times the number of EHCPs every month than they were before. “The problem for us all is the demand for EHCPs is much greater than that and it’s grown rapidly in recent years.” Cllr Nethsingha’s amendment passed – with 28 votes for, 23 against and one abstention – but she then urged members to vote against it. She said the motion would still require the council to undergo a review, as she could not change this, and this would delay progress on improving wait times. She said: “The things that have been recommended in this motion would not help with actually declining the backlogs. “They would put an additional burden on the staff who are desperately trying to deal with these issues for children and families.” Cllr Tom Sanderson, chair of the meeting, told members they would have to vote on the motion within four minutes due to a strict two and a half hour time limit on motions. “After a number of councillors raised issues with this and asked for clarification, Cllr Sanderson said that time had run out and the motion was dropped.

metadata.title: St Neots Hockey Club’s first teams win as seven sides record mixed results
metadata.contentSnippet: St Neots Hockey Club recorded three victories, two draws and two defeats across its men’s and women’s teams.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots Hockey Club’s first teams win as seven sides record mixed results
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: St Neots Hockey Club recorded three victories, two draws and two defeats across its men’s and women’s teams. The Men’s 1s beat Cambridge University 4s 4-1 after conceding five minutes into the match. Phil McMorris levelled during the first half before Rory Jones put St Neots ahead after half-time. McMorris scored twice during the second half to complete his hat-trick and secure the win. The Women’s 1s defeated Cambridge South 2s 2-0. Belle Holmes opened the scoring in the 16th minute, while Kira Herbert added the second goal during the second half. St Neots also kept a clean sheet. The Men’s 2s drew 2-2 away to Cambridge South 4s. Sami Farrer equalised after receiving an aerial assist from Iain Moor. Cambridge South regained the lead before half-time. St Neots continued to create pressure and Henry Milner scored from a short corner late in the match to earn a point. The Men’s 3s drew 1-1 with Newmarket 3s. Newmarket scored shortly after half-time, but Sam Douglas equalised late in the match. The Men’s 4s secured a 1-0 win against Kettering 5s. Eddie Penrose scored in the 11th minute, with the goal proving enough to secure the points. The Women’s 2s lost 4-3 away to Haverhill. After Haverhill scored early, Ness Wilson put St Neots ahead by scoring twice inside the opening 10 minutes. Wilson completed her hat-trick during the second half. Haverhill scored the winning goal two minutes before the end of the match. The Women’s 3s lost 3-2 away to Newmarket. St Neots fell three goals behind early in the second half before Charlotte Duberly and Sarah Leyshon scored. The two goals set up a late fightback, but St Neots could not find an equaliser. The results leave the club with wins across both first teams, a win for the Men’s 4s and points from both men’s reserve fixtures.

metadata.title: St Ives beat St Neots 14-7 in hard-fought local derby on narrow pitch
metadata.contentSnippet: St Ives extended their winning run with a hard-fought victory over local rivals St Neots in testing conditions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ives beat St Neots 14-7 in hard-fought local derby on narrow pitch
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: St Ives extended their winning run with a hard-fought victory over local rivals St Neots in testing conditions. The league fixture was played at St Neots, where prolonged dry weather forced the match on to a narrow pitch. The Bulls prevailed seven points to fourteen, with Henri Cole and Ben Peach scoring tries, both converted by Charlie Mandley and Dan Hawkins respectively. The main pitch had been cordoned off before kick-off, leaving both sides to adapt quickly to unfamiliar surroundings. The restricted width encouraged a direct contest, with the teams relying heavily on their forwards and struggling to remain inside the touchlines. St Neots used the wind well during the opening half, with their powerful carriers and midfield runners forcing Ives deep into their own territory. Josh Meadows produced several important ankle-level tackles, disrupting a number of promising attacks from the home side. The scoreboard remained blank after half an hour, but Ives then produced a sustained spell of possession lasting at least 25 rucks. St Neots defended stubbornly, yet their resistance finally ended when Cole stepped between two defenders and crossed beneath the posts. Ben Peach (Image: Paul Cox) Charlie Mandley converted to give the visitors a seven-point advantage at the interval. Ives hoped the wind at their backs would allow them to take control after the restart, although conditions also contributed to several misplaced passes. The visitors gained increasing authority at the set piece, with Ben Peach particularly effective in the lineout. Peach won opposition possession as well as securing accurate throws from Ives hooker Sam Marjason-Stamp. The Bulls’ pack continued to make ground and, late in the third quarter, drove towards the line before Peach forced his way over. Hawkins added the conversion to put Ives two scores ahead. St Neots responded by attacking with greater urgency, but the visitors defended resolutely, with replacement Matt Holland making a notable contribution. The hosts did pull a converted try back after a miskicked ball was carried backwards by the wind and returned unexpectedly to their winger. He ran in unopposed, but Ives held firm during the closing stages to secure victory. Director of rugby, Duncan Williams, said: “It was a really close game which we ultimately never looked like losing. “It was disappointing to only get four points but we are happy with the win and look ahead to playing second-placed Stewarts & Lloyds next week.”

metadata.title: 'Vile predator' subjected girl to 'horrific' sexual assault on train

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "vile predator" from Cambridgeshire who followed a teenage girl through a station and subjected her to a prolonged sexual assault has been jailed. Bradley Warby, 41, was in King’s Cross railway station when he noticed a 16-year-old girl standing with her mother in a queue for coffee. He approached them and spoke to the girl briefly before she walked away with her mother on April 25. Warby then followed them through the station, at which point the girl's mother told him that her daughter was 16. He stopped following them, but after boarding the train to Peterborough he noticed the victim was sat by herself nearby. He beckoned for her to come over and sit with him, but she moved away. Warby followed the girl and sat next to her, repeatedly attempting to speak to her and made sexual comments towards her. He then repeatedly sexually assaulted her before getting off the train at Peterborough. A concerned bystander who noticed the incident reported it to British Transport Police by texting 61016. Detectives investigating the crime report were able to identify Warby through CCTV images, and he was arrested on August 5. In police interview he claimed the victim had lied about the encounter. Warby, of Caldecote Close, Peterborough, was sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court to one year and two months in prison on October 5. He pleaded guilty at a previous hearing to three counts of sexual assault Detective Constable John Severns said: "Bradley Warby is a vile sexual predator who singled out a teenage girl and subjected her to a horrific sexual assault. "I hope he spends his time in prison reflecting on his criminal actions, and that his conviction grants the victim some sense of closure after what he put her through. "Behaviour like Warby exhibited is simply unacceptable, and we will stop at nothing to put sex offenders like him before the courts to face justice. "Anyone who experiences or witnesses this offending on the railway is urged to report it to us by texting 61016, or calling 999 in an emergency." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire residents recycle nearly 4,000 tonnes of electrical waste
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire residents recycled nearly 4,000 tonnes of electrical waste through household recycling centres last year. The figure, recorded between April 2025 and March 2026, highlights efforts to tackle electronic waste and promote sustainability across the county. Cllr Ros Hathorn, Chair of the Environment and Green Investment Committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "We’re delighted that local residents have taken such positive action and recycled so many items of waste electrical and electronic equipment, which allows these items to be disposed of safely or recycled. "We are dedicated to supporting local people and communities to reduce waste and reuse materials, as well as supporting initiatives that help with climate change." Of the total collected, 603 tonnes were fridges and 442 tonnes were computer monitors. All items were classified as WEEE (waste electrical and electronic equipment), covering everything from large appliances like washing machines and ovens to smaller items such as kettles and toasters. The council also reminded residents that items containing batteries, such as disposable vapes, earbuds, and power banks, should be taken to recycling centres.

metadata.title: Calls for urgent upgrade to pipe network after ‘brutal’ summer of ‘record leaks’
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire County Council agreed to write to the government and regulators to request water companies work with councils on highway impacts, leaks and infrastructure planning at a meeting last week.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Calls for urgent upgrade to pipe network after ‘brutal’ summer of ‘record leaks’
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council has called for greater collaboration with water and utility companies for an “urgent” upgrade of pipes following “record numbers of leaks”. Cambridgeshire County Council agreed to write to the government and regulators to request water companies work with councils on highway impacts, leaks and infrastructure planning at a meeting last week. Cllr Ros Hathorn said the summer’s heatwaves have been “absolutely brutal” to the pipes and moving into winter “the freeze-thaw cycle always punishes the pipes”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “There’s probably no community in the county that hasn’t experienced a trickle or a torrent of water from a burst water pipe this summer.” Cllr Hathorn, of Histon, Impington, Orchard Park and King’s Meadow, said water companies need to upgrade the system rather than patching leaks as they happen. She said: “Emergency repairs are the worst way to maintain infrastructure and that is what is happening – it’s expensive, wasteful and disruptive. “It’s clear from the number of leaks and the age of our roads that there is an urgent need for a planned upgrade of the water pipes in our road. “For far too long, we haven’t paid attention to investing in our water infrastructure.” Cllr Ian Manning, of Chesterton, said a neighbour had questioned him on why roadworks weren’t coordinated after his wife faced delays returning from work. The Lib Dem councillor said they “simply don’t have the powers” but supported the “dig once initiative” to make different companies coordinate works so they happen at the same time. He said: “If only we could have a bit of weight behind it and the power to get all these different companies to coordinate at the same time and not have to repair the roads over and over again”. Cllr Yannifer Malinowski, of Burwell, said the growth of Cambridge and surrounding areas must be accompanied with suitable infrastructure. The Lib Dem councillor said that summer saw “record numbers of leaks and extensive road closures across the county”. She said: “We need to ask whether enough is being done to address the root causes rather than always dealing with the consequences and patching up their failures.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Man accused of Huntingdon train stabbings pleads guilty to wounding with intent
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man accused of a mass stabbing on a train in Huntingdon, and separate attacks earlier that day in London and the day before in Peterborough, has pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder and is due to stand trial next week. Passengers and staff were injured on a service from Doncaster to London on November 1 after it left Peterborough, leading to an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon railway station. Anthony Williams pleaded guilty at Cambridge Crown Court today. (Image: Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire) At a pre-trial review hearing at Cambridge Crown Court today (October 19), Williams pleaded guilty to 14 new counts, 12 of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent. He was also rearraigned on seven counts to which he had previously pleaded not guilty. Williams pleaded guilty to affray at a barber shop in Peterborough on October 31 and the theft of knives from an Asda store in Stevenage on October 31. He pleaded guilty to possessing a bladed article in a public place at a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk, the Rail World car park and Queen’s Walk in Peterborough on October 31. Williams pleaded guilty to 14 new counts, 12 of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent. (Image: Joe Giddens) He admitted possession of a bladed article at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London in the early hours of November 1. Williams pleaded guilty to a common assault on a Govia Thameslink train travelling between St Pancras station and Biggleswade station on November 1. He pleaded guilty to possession of a knife on a train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on November 1. He also pleaded guilty to the assault occasioning actual bodily harm of a male police officer in custody on November 2. Passengers and staff were injured on a service from Doncaster to London on November 1. (Image: Chris Radburn/PA Wire) Williams, who appeared at today's hearing on a video-link from custody, entered pleas of not guilty at an earlier hearing to 10 counts of attempted murder after several people were stabbed on an LNER train from Doncaster to London on the evening of November 1 last year. He denies one count of attempted murder over an incident at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London on November 1. He also denies the attempted murders of a 14-year-old boy, a 22-year-old man, and a 28-year-old man in Peterborough on October 31. Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said: “Those guilty pleas do not resolve the indictment so there will be a trial.” The judge, Mr Justice Calver, said Williams would stand trial in relation to the remaining counts from Monday, October 26.

metadata.title: Optometrists prepare for second Ghana trip to provide free eye care in rural villages
metadata.contentSnippet: A team of optometrists from St Neots is preparing for a life-changing journey to Ghana.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Optometrists prepare for second Ghana trip to provide free eye care in rural villages
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A team of optometrists is preparing for a life-changing journey to Ghana. The group, from St Neots, Bedford, Dunstable, and Biggleswade, will travel to the Ashanti region of Ghana this November to deliver essential eye care in rural communities. They will spend two weeks in the village of Gyetiase, providing free eye tests and glasses with the support of charity Ashanti Development. Shivam Patel, ophthalmic director at Specsavers in St Neots, said: "We would love the local community to get behind us again by donating any old or unwanted glasses they no longer need. "Every pair we can take with us gives us another opportunity to help someone see more clearly. "Something that may have been sitting unused in a drawer here can genuinely help transform another person’s daily life." This will be the team’s second visit to Ghana. During their previous trip, they examined 1,333 people, distributed more than 1,000 pairs of glasses, and helped fund 72 cataract surgeries. Access to eye care can be extremely limited in rural areas, and for many people this will be their first eye test. Specsavers customers are being encouraged to donate old or unwanted glasses, which will be distributed during the visit. A major focus of the trip is raising funds for cataract surgery. A specialist surgical team will join the project in its second week to operate on patients identified during initial screenings. Shivam said: "Whether someone donates a pair of glasses, contributes a few pounds to the fundraising appeal or simply helps us spread the word, every bit of support matters." Glasses donations can be made at Specsavers St Neots, 13 High Street, St Neots, Cambridgeshire, PE19 1BU. To support the fundraising appeal, visit www.gofund.me/80505b29f.

metadata.title: Meet the medical tattooist who helps surgery and cancer patients reclaim confidence
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire medical tattooist Helen Honey helps surgery, cancer and trauma patients restore confidence with scar camouflage and 3D areola tattoos in Ely.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Meet the medical tattooist who helps surgery and cancer patients reclaim confidence
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A permanent make-up artist from Cambridgeshire is using her skills to help people heal after surgery, trauma, and cancer treatment. Ely-based Helen Honey runs The Brow & Body Studio, which offers medical tattooing, scar restoration, areola reconstruction, and camouflage services from her private studio. She said: "It helps not only repair the body but restore people's confidence, whether they're recovering from an accident, surgery or trauma." Her decision to expand into medical tattooing followed the loss of a close family friend to cancer in 2020, which prompted her to consider how her skills could support those dealing with more than just cosmetic concerns. After extensive research, she undertook specialist training in areola reconstruction, scar and stretch-mark restoration, and scar camouflage. Helen working in the studio (Image: Helen Honey) Ms Honey said: "I am so grateful to be able to be a part of each patient's healing journey. "My friend had to make the life-changing decision of having a voluntary double mastectomy after being diagnosed with the BRCA gene. "I had the honour of helping her through part of her cancer journey by doing 3D areola tattoo restoration, something that is no longer available on the NHS." Her services include MCA (Multi-Trepannic Collagen Actuation), an inkless needling technique that uses medical-grade needles to create micro-trauma, stimulating collagen production and helping to improve the appearance of scars, burns, and stretch marks. Clients have included individuals recovering from mastectomies, breast augmentation, body contouring surgery, burns, gender-affirming procedures, and significant weight-loss journeys. Each treatment takes place in Ms Honey’s private studio in Ely, which she believes offers clients a safe and comfortable environment to share their stories and begin their healing journey. A patient's before and after photos (Image: Helen Honey) She said: "Many clients arrive anxious or self-conscious, carrying difficult memories, and a private, one-to-one setting gives them space for the kind of sensitive conversation that rarely happens in a busy salon." Ms Honey’s work was recently recognised at the 2026 UK PMU Awards, the UK’s largest permanent make-up awards event, where she was named a top 10 finalist in the Medical Artist of the Year category. She said: "It was the most educational and emotional weekend. "I'm so grateful for the recognition, as it's so complicated but so emotionally rewarding." Her skills recently helped a Cambridgeshire man regain confidence after life-saving surgery left him with a large abdominal scar and no belly button. Following several sessions of MCA to soften the scar tissue, Ms Honey used medical tattooing techniques to recreate a realistic, three-dimensional belly button. Her journey into permanent make-up began after she left a long corporate career to pursue a career that offered greater work-life balance. What started as a creative venture soon became a mission to help others through restorative and medical tattooing. She continues to expand her expertise and is set to introduce laser tattoo removal to her list of services from the end of October. Ms Honey said: "I just want people to know what I can do for them. "To be able to make people happy and confident in themselves again – this job enables me to do just that." In recognition of Breast Cancer Awareness Month, she is offering 20 per cent off areola tattooing services until the end of October, with all consultations provided free of charge. Appointments can be booked by emailing thebrowandbodystudio@gmail.com. Ms Honey’s work highlights the growing impact of medical tattooing, not just in cosmetic enhancement but in supporting emotional and psychological recovery. By combining technical skill with compassion, she is helping individuals reclaim confidence and comfort in their bodies after life-changing events. The Brow & Body Studio continues to evolve, now offering a wider range of restorative and aesthetic treatments designed to support healing and self-esteem. Ms Honey said: "This work goes far beyond beauty. "It's about giving people the chance to feel whole again."

metadata.title: Family's tribute to 'beautiful, loving son' who died in lorry crash
metadata.contentSnippet: The family of a motorcyclist from Yaxley who was tragically killed in a crash involving a lorry in Sawtry have paid tribute to a "beautiful, loving son".

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Family's tribute to 'beautiful, loving son' who died in lorry crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The family of a motorcyclist who was tragically killed in a crash involving a lorry have paid tribute to a "beautiful, loving son". Tyler Ellis was riding a black Kawaski motorbike when it was involved in a collision with a red Volvo HGV. The incident happened on the B1043 Old North Road in Sawtry at about 12.50pm October 5. The 23-year-old, of Royce Close, Yaxley, died at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge the following day. The driver of the HGV, a 76-year-old man from Wisbech, was uninjured. He was arrested at the scene on suspicion of causing serious injury by careless driving and has since been bailed until January 4, 2027. Paying tribute, his family said: "Today, we pay tribute to our beautiful, loving son, whose life was tragically taken following a road traffic collision. "Tyler was loved beyond words by his family and friends. "He was such a kind, loving and likeable young man, with a smile that could light up any room and a laugh that was truly infectious. "He had a special way of bringing happiness to those around him, and his presence made life brighter for everyone who knew him. "There are simply no words to describe the heartbreak and devastation we feel at losing our precious boy." They added: "Our world has been shattered in a way that words can never explain, and there will forever be an emptiness in our hearts that can never be filled. "Tyler, you were taken from us far too soon, and we will carry you in our hearts every single day. "The love we have for you will never fade, and although we cannot hold you in our arms, you will forever be a part of us. "Your memories, your smile and your laughter will live on in everyone who was lucky enough to know you. "Fly high, our beautiful boy. Until we meet again, may you rest peacefully, knowing just how deeply you are loved and how terribly you will be missed. "Forever our son, forever in our hearts, forever 23. "Rest in peace, Tyler. We love you always." We have opened a Book of Condolence for Tyler Ellis, a "beautiful, loving son" who tragically died in a crash involving a lorry in Sawtry. This is for anyone who wants to leave a tribute to Tyler or condolences for his loved ones. Please know we will moderate content to ensure it remains a respectful space. There may be a delay in messages being made public as they require approval.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire stalker has been jailed after refusing to accept the end of a month-long relationship. Jamie Keegan, 38, of Vars Road, Hampton Hargate, Peterborough, began harassing the woman in December 2024 after she ended the relationship. Keegan became angry and verbally abusive, sending her a barrage of messages and threatening to take his own life. Despite the victim’s efforts to remain supportive, Keegan continued to pursue a romantic relationship and became angry when she made it clear she wanted to be nothing more than friends. When she tried to cut contact completely, he threatened to harm himself. After she blocked him on social media, Keegan created fake accounts to keep messaging her. In December 2025, the victim told Keegan to leave her alone, but he bombarded her with messages and voice notes, some abusive. He also sent pictures of himself after harming himself and again threatened to take his own life. Keegan’s behaviour escalated when he discovered where she lived and sent her a picture of himself holding rope nearby. He also contacted her family, friends and workplace, forcing colleagues to walk her to her car after work. In a police interview, Keegan admitted sending a “high volume of messages” to get “some accountability” from the victim. Jamie Keegan became angry and verbally abusive at the victim (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) On October 15, at Cambridge Crown Court, he was sentenced to two years and two months in prison after admitting stalking involving serious alarm or distress. Detective Constable Ryan Burke said: "Keegan simply refused to accept that the victim did not want a relationship with him. "She repeatedly made her wishes clear and tried to cut contact, but he continued to pursue her, creating fake accounts and contacting her friends, family and workplace. "His relentless behaviour caused her serious distress and affected her day-to-day life, including leaving her reliant on colleagues to walk her to her car after work. “This case is a reminder that if someone tells you they do not want contact, you must respect that. "Repeated unwanted contact is not romantic or persistent affection, it can amount to stalking.”

metadata.title: MP urges Energy Secretary to reject East Park solar farm plans near villages
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty has urged the Government’s new Energy Secretary to consider local concerns before deciding the fate of the proposed East Park Energy solar farm.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP urges Energy Secretary to reject East Park solar farm plans near villages
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty has urged the Government’s new Energy Secretary to consider local concerns before deciding the fate of the proposed East Park Energy solar farm. Ben Obese-Jecty said he had repeatedly pressed ministers for answers about the 1,900-acre scheme, which would run from north Bedfordshire into Huntingdonshire and affect villages including Great Staughton and Hail Weston. The project is being considered as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP), meaning the final decision will be made by the Secretary of State following recommendations from the Planning Inspectorate. Mr Obese-Jecty said previous energy ministers had declined to comment on the application because of its status within the planning process. Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty has urged the Government's new Energy Secretary to consider local concerns before deciding on a proposed East Park Energy Solar Farm. (Image: Stop East Park Energy) (Image: Stop East Park Energy) Following a recent ministerial reshuffle, he has now written to Miatta Fahnbulleh, the newly appointed Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, outlining what he described as the project's impact on local communities. In an October 7 letter, the MP said he supported expanding renewable energy but believed the East Park Energy scheme was unsuitable because of its size and location. He said about 74 per cent of the 1,900-acre site is Best and Most Versatile agricultural land, including Grade 2 and Grade 3a farmland, and warned that covering it with solar panels could threaten food production and food security. The MP also claimed the development, together with other existing and approved solar schemes in the area, would create an industrial-scale solar corridor approaching 2,800 acres. He said residents of Hail Weston and Great Staughton feared the scheme would alter the character of the rural landscape. The letter also warned of a 30-to-36-month construction programme, more heavy lorries on rural roads, flooding caused by soil compaction and runoff, and damage to wildlife corridors and public rights of way. Mr Obese-Jecty said he hoped ministers would listen to local people before deciding the scheme’s fate. He said: "With a decision expected in the coming weeks, though not clear when, I hope that the Government will take heed of local concerns before making a final decision on whether to go ahead." A decision on the East Park Energy Development Consent Order application is expected later this year. The developer says the scheme could generate up to 400 megawatts, enough to supply approximately 108,000 homes, and would operate for 40 years before decommissioning. The developer says solar panels would cover around 57% of the land across the four sites, with the remainder used for planting, screening, habitat creation and access.

metadata.title: Exact time clocks change in the UK this weekend and why they change
metadata.contentSnippet: Clocks will go back across the UK this weekend on Sunday, October 25 at 2am, marking the end of British Summer Time and an extra hour in bed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Exact time clocks change in the UK this weekend and why they change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Clocks across the UK will turn back one hour this weekend. The change takes place at 2am on Sunday, October 25, when clocks go back across the country. Moving the hands back gives an extra hour in bed for a Sunday lie-in. It also provides an hour of sunlight as November approaches and days shorten. People will not need to alter timepieces by hand in most cases. Devices connected to the internet update automatically, including smartphones, laptops, tablets and televisions. Alarm clocks, car radios and equipment not connected to the internet will require manual adjustment. The purpose of the system is to make use of daylight. Germany introduced the first clock change in 1916 during the First World War to save energy. Less electricity was needed when daylight lasted longer. Britain and European governments followed, which began British Summer Time. The system has remained in place in the UK since 1971.

metadata.title: Rare Royal Mint 50p coin sells for more than 400 times face value on eBay
metadata.contentSnippet: A rare 2009 Kew Gardens 50p coin has sold for £213.50 on eBay after drawing 18 bids, fetching more than 400 times its original face value.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare Royal Mint 50p coin sells for more than 400 times face value on eBay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare 50p coin has fetched more than 400 times its face value after an online auction. The Kew Gardens piece drew 18 bids on eBay before being snapped up for £213.50. Released by the Royal Mint in 2009, only 210,000 copies of the coin were ever produced. The coin was introduced to celebrate the 250th anniversary of London's famous royal botanical garden. Its reverse design by Christopher Le Brun features the famous Chinese Pagoda entwined with a decorative climber, alongside the portrait of Queen Elizabeth II on the obverse. The piece has long been regarded as one of the most sought-after coins in modern British circulation. A low initial mintage combined with intense collector demand means very few examples remain in everyday circulation. The 50p piece provides a distinct heptagonal canvas for coin designers. With a diameter of 27.5mm, it is the largest British coin in circulation and offers space for commemorative artwork. Rarity serves as the primary factor driving collector demand and market prices. Low mintage figures mean fewer examples exist to buy or trade. Coin condition also plays an important role, with well-preserved specimens securing higher prices. Collectors also prize unusual design errors and striking flaws that escape the mint. Sales avenues can influence the price realised for a rare coin. Sellers often turn to competitive online bidding on eBay to test market demand. Others prefer formal valuations from professional coin dealers to establish a certified market value. Royal Mint mintage figures confirm the rarest 50p designs to enter general circulation: The 2023 Atlantic Salmon coin holds the title as the rarest 50p design in circulation. Anyone checking their loose change is urged to keep an eye out for these scarce editions.

metadata.title: Funding secured to continue support for frequent A&E attendees in Cambs
metadata.contentSnippet: More than £600,000 in funding has been secured to continue a life-changing support service in Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Funding secured to continue support for frequent A&E attendees in Cambs
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than £600,000 in funding has been secured to continue a life-changing support service in Cambridgeshire. The High Impact Use (HIU) service, which helps people with complex needs reduce A&E visits, is designed for those whose frequent emergency department attendances are often linked to social, emotional, or practical challenges rather than purely medical issues. Cambridgeshire County Council has secured £609,552 for the 2027/28 financial year through a new agreement with the NHS Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Integrated Care Board (ICB). Councillor Alison Whelan, chair of the council’s communities, social mobility and inclusion committee, said: "The High Impact Use service shows what's possible when organisations work together to support residents in a more personalised and preventative way. "Many of the people supported by the service face complex challenges that cannot be resolved through healthcare interventions alone. "By helping residents access the right support at the right time, we can improve outcomes for individuals, helping them live independently and create stronger ties, while also reducing demand on our hospitals and emergency services." Launched in October 2024, the HIU service has already shown promising results. According to the ICB, health-related costs for an initial group of service users dropped from an average of £18,333 per person per year to £3,401 per person per year after receiving support. Cambridgeshire County Council is the only local authority in the country to directly host a High Impact Use service. The scheme has gained national attention, including a visit from NHS England representatives who highlighted the service as a strong example of community-led practice. It has also received an Outstanding Achievement Award from North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust. The new funding will allow the council to continue hosting the HIU Operational Team throughout the 2027/28 financial year in partnership with the ICB, local hospitals, and the East of England Ambulance Service.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Parents hoping to keep October half-term costs down can get free or £1 meals for children at a host of restaurants, pubs and supermarket cafés – with some offers available across the UK. Ben Smye, deals expert at HotUKDeals.com, said: “Families across the UK are preparing for another expensive school break. “Luckily, restaurants and supermarkets are stepping up again with free meals and £1 deals that can slash the cost of spending family time together.” (Image: Getty Images) Burger King is running its Kids Eat Free offer from now until November 1. Families can claim a free King Jr. Meal through the Burger King UK app when an adult buys a qualifying burger meal at a participating restaurant. Children can choose from a Whopper Jr., Hamburger, Cheeseburger or Chicken Nuggets, with a kids' drink and a choice of sides included. The offer excludes certain adult meals, including King Savers, Cheeseburgers, Hamburgers, bundles and Melts burgers. It is not valid at motorway service locations, airports, train stations or holiday parks, and cannot be combined with other promotions. Several popular restaurant chains are running free-meal promotions during the school break, although the dates differ by location. Bella Italia, Frankie & Benny’s, Banana Tree and Las Iguanas are offering Kids Eat Free during the October half-term, giving families an affordable way to enjoy a meal out together as the colder days return. (Image: Bella Italia) Other chains have offers that can help families keep costs down beyond the main half-term promotion dates. (Image: Morrisons) Families looking for a cheaper lunch can also turn to supermarket cafés and other retailers. Prezzo has three offers for families this October half-term, including a deal aimed specifically at teenagers. Prezzo is also donating £1 to BBC Children in Need for every new Kids Club subscription redeemed during the campaign. Children can enjoy activities, 3D menus and Pudsey-themed fun at the table. The campaign starts on October 12 in Scotland and October 19 in the rest of the UK. Check the offer terms and participating restaurants before visiting. Families heading out early can also find savings on breakfast. Toby Carvery is also running a £1 children's meal offer from October 10 to November 1, including weekends. Children can get a main meal, carvery or breakfast for £1 with an adult main meal or all-you-can-eat breakfast, subject to the offer's terms and app or sign-up requirements. Recommended reading Clair Hughes, Savings Expert at VoucherCodes.co.uk, said families should look beyond the headline offer to work out how much they will really save. She advised checking the price of the adult meal and any extras, as some promotions require a full-price main while others include drinks, sides or dessert. Families should also check how many children's meals can be claimed per paying adult, and plan to use the offers on days when they were already intending to eat out. Hughes said discounted gift cards could offer another saving where the terms allow them to be used alongside a kids-eat-free promotion. For example, she said a £40 Bella Italia gift card could be bought for £36 through VoucherCodes, saving £4 before the free children's meal is taken into account. She also recommended checking loyalty apps, which may unlock further offers. Families are advised to check the offer's full terms and confirm that their local restaurant or café is participating before setting off. Offers can be subject to availability, age limits, minimum spends, exclusions and restrictions on combining discounts.

metadata.title: 91-year-old railway enthusiast returns to steam trains after regaining mobility
metadata.contentSnippet: A 91-year-old train enthusiast has returned to the railways after regaining his mobility in Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 91-year-old railway enthusiast returns to steam trains after regaining mobility
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A 91-year-old train enthusiast has returned to the railways after regaining his mobility in Cambridgeshire. Peter Brown, who spent 40 years working on the railways, travelled by steam train from Sheringham to Holt on the Poppy Line in Norfolk, a journey made possible thanks to rehabilitation at Bramley Court Care Home in Histon. Mr Brown said: "I had given up when I came to Bramley. Staff at Bramley Court helped make the special journey possible (Image: Bramley Court Care Home) "I’d been in hospital for so long and everything was unknown." He dislocated both shoulders in a fall at his Cambridge home earlier this year and spent five months in hospital before moving to the care home in June. With support from staff and his family, he began a rehabilitation programme that included weekly physiotherapy, exercise classes, and daily walking practice. The 91-year-old enjoyed a special journey on the Poppy Line (Image: Bramley Court Care Home) Carol Morgan, head of quality at Bramley Court, said: "Peter was using a wheelchair when he came to us, but just three months later, he was walking with a frame. "He has also regained the use of his arms and he has his independence back." The trip, taken alongside his two daughters, brought back fond memories of his career on the railways. The railway trip brought back memories of Peter’s 40-year career. (Image: Bramley Court Care Home) Mr Brown began working in 1951, starting as a fireman on steam trains before moving to diesel locomotives and becoming a driver in the 1980s. He said: "I couldn’t move my shoulders or hold a cup, and I couldn’t get out of bed. "I didn’t think I’d get to where I am now including being able to walk down the train platform. Rehabilitation helped Peter regain his mobility and independence (Image: Bramley Court Care Home) "Now, when I walk, I feel so happy I could run." The care home, which provides residential, nursing, and dementia care, is currently taking part in a research study with Care England on supporting people whose mobility has reduced following hospital admission.

metadata.title: 10 Cambs high-rise buildings which need cladding replaced include fire station
metadata.contentSnippet: The ten high-rise buildings in Cambridgeshire that still need “unsafe cladding” replaced have been revealed, with one being directly attached to a fire station.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 Cambs high-rise buildings which need cladding replaced include fire station
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. The ten high-rise buildings that still need “unsafe cladding” replaced have been revealed, with one being directly attached to a fire station. A meeting of the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority last month revealed there are still residential buildings of seven stories or more waiting for replacement works. The authority said they were “confident” they will meet the government deadline of December 31, 2029, for all high-rises to have their cladding replaced. This was set after the conclusion of the inquiry into the Grenfell Tower fire in 2017 when 72 people lost their lives in the fire which spread through flammable cladding. The inquiry concluded in 2025 and also set a deadline of December 31, 2031, for medium-rise residential buildings to have any unsafe cladding replaced. The combined authority was told that the buildings identified belong to private owners, whose responsibility it is to replace the cladding. A new bill was brought to Parliament this week which, if approved, will give councils more power to replace cladding themselves if the building’s owners fail to act. The Remediation of Unsafe Cladding Bill will also place a legal duty on owners to fix issues without delay or they may face criminal penalties – including a fine of up to £500k. A Freedom of Information request to the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority has revealed the buildings which are still waiting for unsafe cladding to be replaced. It includes all of the Parkside Place development – with Cambridge Fire Station on its lower floor – and the Parkside Terrace building is the tallest on the list at eight stories. All ten buildings are in Cambridge with the remaining being Petersfield House in Parkside Place, the Cyan Building, 1-32 Orchid Building and the Aqua Building on Glenalmond Avenue, Meade House on Mill Park, The Lauro Building on Aberdeen Avenue and The Triangle Blocks A, B and C on Warren Close. There are also 84 medium-rise residential buildings waiting for cladding to be replaced. A spokesperson for the combined authority said that even if a building is waiting for unsafe cladding to be replaced, it does not mean the building is unsafe to live in. They said: “There may be mitigating measures in place, such as changes to the fire alarm system so that everyone is alerted to a fire at the same time, and would all leave the building together (called simultaneous evacuation). “This will be determined by the external wall report completed by a qualified fire engineer.” They said that five buildings have had replacement works completed, two are currently having work done and work is set to start on 14 more buildings in the next two months. A further update will be presented to the combined authority’s growth committee in November. They said: “We are supporting responsible entities to meet their obligations on building remediation, and where they are not doing so, regulators will take appropriate action. “For any buildings undergoing remediation, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service has a webpage with fire safety advice for members of the public: Fire safety advice during building remediation.”

metadata.title: Clinical hypnotherapist explains why driving can make people feel anxious
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire-based clinical hypnotherapist Dan Regan explains why driving can make people feel anxious.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Clinical hypnotherapist explains why driving can make people feel anxious
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire-based clinical hypnotherapist Dan Regan explains why driving can make people feel anxious As the evenings draw in, driving can become more uncomfortable for some people. Darker roads, headlight glare, wet weather and reduced visibility can all make journeys feel more difficult than they did during the summer. But driving anxiety certainly isn't limited to driving in the dark. One thing I've noticed from working with people with driving anxiety is just how differently it can affect people. Someone might be perfectly happy driving around Ely or on familiar local roads but avoid dual carriageways or motorways altogether. For someone else, it might be particular situations such as joining a fast road, overtaking, busy roads or driving somewhere unfamiliar. Some people may become anxious about almost any journey. And I've also worked with people who are comfortable driving themselves but become very anxious when they're a passenger and someone else is in control. The anxiety itself can vary too. For some, there's a constant feeling of tension or unease. Others might experience a racing heart, shaking, dizziness, feeling hot or other physical symptoms of anxiety. If someone has experienced a panic attack while driving, they can understandably become very worried about it happening again. And often the anxiety begins long before even getting into the car. You might start worrying about a journey hours or even days beforehand. You imagine the difficult parts of the journey, wonder how you'll feel and start thinking about what you'll do if the anxiety becomes too much. By the time you actually get into the car, you've already spent a lot of time practising feeling anxious about the journey. Avoidance can then creep in. Perhaps you choose a longer route because it avoids a dual carriageway, only drive at quieter times or ask somebody else to drive. You may stop travelling somewhere altogether because getting there feels too difficult. Those decisions can make perfect sense in the moment because they reduce the anxiety. But repeatedly avoiding something because of anxiety can reinforce the idea that it was something you needed to avoid. Gradually, your world can become a little smaller. Driving anxiety can affect much more than simply how comfortable you feel behind the wheel. It can affect work, seeing friends and family, days out, holidays and your independence. That's why I tend to look beyond simply trying to make someone “feel confident” about driving. I'm interested in the patterns that have developed around it. For example, what are you imagining before a journey? What are you paying attention to while you're driving? What are you doing to try to prevent yourself from feeling anxious? And what have you gradually started avoiding? Those patterns can become very well practised, but that doesn't mean they have to stay that way. So if driving has become more uncomfortable as the nights draw in, it may be worth noticing not only how anxious you feel, but also what you're doing in response to that anxiety. And if your driving has gradually become restricted to certain roads, routes or situations, remember that those patterns can change. You don't necessarily have to accept those restrictions as your new normal. Dan Regan is a clinical hypnotherapist specialising in anxiety, based in Ely and Newmarket. You can find more anxiety help and information at danreganhypnotherapy.co.uk

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire-led study to recruit 7,500 people to improve psychosis care
metadata.contentSnippet: A major research programme to improve early intervention in psychosis is being led by Cambridgeshire and Peterborough.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire-led study to recruit 7,500 people to improve psychosis care
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major research programme to improve early intervention in psychosis is being led by Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. The Early Intervention Mission, spearheaded by Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust (CPFT), is a UK-wide study focused on early identification, monitoring and personalised care for individuals experiencing a first episode of psychosis. Symptoms of psychosis can include hallucinations, hearing voices, delusions and disorganised thinking. Professor Graham Murray, consultant psychiatrist at CPFT and professor of psychiatry and neuroscience at the University of Cambridge, said: "This research will help us understand who is at risk of early psychosis and how best to target preventative treatment and tailor personalised mental health care to meet their needs. "Working with expert colleagues across the UK, we’re on a mission to use new digital technologies, electronic health records and genetic data to improve care and treatment, and support recovery. "Effective early intervention can give people a much better quality of life." The study aims to recruit up to 7,500 people in the early stages of psychosis, along with up to 500 healthy control participants. Participants identified through health service records will be invited to take part remotely via NHS England’s DigiTrials service. Where suitable, individuals may be asked to attend an initial research visit to provide a blood or saliva sample and complete questionnaires and cognitive tasks. Those with psychosis will be followed every six months for up to three years using digital questionnaires. Data collected will be stored securely in the Mental Health Mission Trusted Research Environment and will be used to investigate factors such as immune markers, genetics and social influences on the development and progression of psychosis. The study is informed by individuals with lived experience and intends to create a long-term, representative resource to support future clinical trials and personalised treatment approaches. It is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research Mental Health Translational Research Collaboration Mission.

Little Paxton Parish Council received the award (for precepts over £25,001) at the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Association of Local Councils (CAPALC) conference. The award recognises the council’s work in delivering inclusive and engaging events for residents, with particular praise given to its Village Adventure Days. Kathy Bishop, chairperson of Little Paxton Parish Council, said: "We are absolutely delighted to receive the CAPALC Council of the Year 2026 (Precept over £25,001) Award. "The Village Adventure Days have been a fantastic way of bringing our community together and providing inclusive activities that residents of all ages can enjoy. "This award is a wonderful recognition of the hard work and commitment of our councillors, staff, volunteers and everyone who has helped make the Adventure Days such a success. "Most importantly, it celebrates our community and the enthusiasm of the residents who have taken part." The Village Adventure Days offer a programme of free activities to encourage community participation and the use of outdoor spaces. Events have featured attractions such as Spider Mountain, Caterpillar Climb, a climbing wall, a bouldering wall, and a mobile skate. The council said the award highlights its commitment to delivering activities that are accessible, inclusive, and welcoming to all. Jenny Gellatly, parish clerk, said: "The award is a tremendous achievement for Little Paxton and provides encouragement to continue developing opportunities that bring residents together and make the village an even more vibrant and inclusive place to live." The council said the Village Adventure Days were designed to promote greater use of the village’s open spaces and provide free adventure experiences for residents. The events were supported by National Lottery Community Fund.

metadata.title: Drum and bass pioneer Goldie to perform at Cambridge Junction
metadata.contentSnippet: Drum and bass pioneer Goldie is set to DJ at the Cambridge Junction on November 11.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drum and bass pioneer Goldie to perform at Cambridge Junction
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drum and bass pioneer Goldie is set to bring his legendary sound to Cambridgeshire. Hosted by promoter Warning, the Metalheadz founder and influential DJ will take to the decks at the Cambridge Junction on the evening of November 11. Goldie, an English music producer, DJ, graffiti artist and actor, first gained recognition through the UK graffiti scene before becoming a pioneering figure in the 1990s jungle, drum and bass and breakbeat hardcore movements. Through projects including Rufige Kru and Metalheads, and as co-founder of the influential Metalheadz label, he helped shape the sound of modern drum and bass. His landmark 1995 album Timeless reached No. 7 in the UK charts and remains one of the genre's defining records. Beyond music, Goldie has enjoyed a successful acting career, appearing in films including the James Bond blockbuster The World Is Not Enough and Guy Ritchie's Snatch, as well as the BBC soap EastEnders. More than three decades after helping define Britain's underground electronic music scene, Goldie remains a major force in dance music, renowned for his high-energy DJ sets and deep knowledge of the culture he helped create. The event is expected to attract drum and bass fans from across the region, with Warning continuing its reputation for bringing some of the genre's biggest names to Cambridge. Tickets are now available online

Construction starts this month on Huntingdon Sport and Health Hub, a £30m project with 3G football, padel and pickleball courts, due autumn 2028. The £30 million hub will provide modern leisure and wellbeing facilities, including a 3G football pitch, padel and pickleball courts, and upgraded health and fitness spaces. Councillor Debbie Mickelburgh, executive councillor for communities, health and leisure, said: "The start of construction is an exciting step forward for the Huntingdon Sport and Health Hub project. "We look forward to seeing the hub take shape and the positive impact it will have in supporting active lifestyles and improving health outcomes for the residents in our district." The hub is part of a wider redevelopment of One Leisure Huntingdon and is expected to deliver more than £1.6 million in wellbeing benefits by getting more young people active. The council has allocated £10.3 million from Community Infrastructure Levy funding to support the project. Construction will continue through to autumn 2028, with the finished hub designed to address health inequalities and encourage lifelong participation in sport. Emma Butler, principal of St Peter’s School, said: "We are delighted that St Peter’s School can play a role in helping to bring this exciting vision to life. "It will create outstanding opportunities for our students to develop their sporting talents, build confidence and enjoy being active, whilst also providing a valuable resource for the wider community." Councillor Patrick Kadewere, mayor of Huntingdon, said: "Huntingdon Town Council is proud to have worked alongside Huntingdonshire District Council, St Peter’s School and the many sports clubs that call this site home to help shape plans for this important investment. "The new Sport and Health Hub will create opportunities for people of all ages to be active, improve their wellbeing, and enjoy sport for generations to come." The district council will work with partners and residents during construction and provide updates as key milestones are reached. The scheme will also expand swimming provision and improve accessibility across the leisure facilities.

metadata.title: Specialist police team recovers almost £700,000 of stolen property in six months
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire Police’s Rural Crime Action Team recovered £699,000 of stolen property, made 26 arrests and tackled vehicle crime from April to September.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Specialist police team recovers almost £700,000 of stolen property in six months
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A specialist police team has recovered nearly £700,000 worth of stolen property in just six months. Cambridgeshire Constabulary’s Rural Crime Action Team (RCAT) made 26 arrests and disrupted organised criminal activity between April and September. They recovered 48 stolen vehicles, trailers, plant machinery and other assets valued at more than £699,000. Sergeant Tom Nuttall, who leads the team, said: "Many people know RCAT as the force's hare coursing team, but that is only one aspect of what we do. "Every day, our officers provide specialist support across Cambridgeshire, from pursuing dangerous offenders and recovering stolen property to locating missing people and assisting with major incidents. "These results highlight the breadth of work undertaken by the team and our continued commitment to protecting rural communities, disrupting organised criminality and supporting the wider policing response across the county." The team also carried out 12 vehicle pursuits and dealt with 107 driving offences. Officers seized 39 uninsured vehicles, recorded 12 drug-possession offences and arrested two people on suspicion of drink-driving. Among the vehicles recovered were 11 cars worth more than £120,000, 13 pick-up vehicles valued at almost £217,000, five items of plant machinery worth £206,000 and three caravans worth more than £46,000. RCAT also supported Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service during major woodland fires over the summer. The team used thermal-imaging drones to identify hotspots, monitor fire behaviour and give firefighters real-time aerial intelligence. The team tackles rural crime year-round, including machinery theft, vehicle crime, drug offences and hare coursing. The team also uses eCops to support operational policing by sharing local alerts and receiving information from residents.

metadata.title: MP calls for social care savings limit to rise from £23,250 for disabled people
metadata.contentSnippet: Ian Sollom MP urges ministers to raise England’s £23,250 social care capital limit, saying outdated rules trap working-age disabled people and block independence.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP calls for social care savings limit to rise from £23,250 for disabled people
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Ian Sollom MP has called on the Government to overhaul social care funding rules which he says are preventing thousands of disabled people from saving for their future and living more independently. The MP for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire has launched a campaign ahead of this month's Autumn Budget, urging the Health Secretary to review the adult social care capital limit after being contacted by constituent Maxwell McKnight, 22. Under current rules, people receiving social care who have more than £23,250 in savings, investments and property can be required to pay the full cost of their care. The upper limit was last increased in 2010/11. Mr Sollom argues the threshold effectively creates a "savings trap" for working-age disabled adults, preventing them from building financial security, saving for a house deposit or planning for the future. According to research cited by the MP, published by The King's Fund, the upper capital limit would now stand at around £35,600 had it risen in line with inflation since 2010/11. Mr McKnight, a wheelchair user who requires round-the-clock care, recently graduated with a first-class degree and now works full-time in central London. He also advocates for disabled people through his online platforms and serves as a trustee of a national disability charity. Mr Sollom said: "Young people like Maxwell have done everything the Government has asked of them under difficult circumstances - studied, worked hard, paid tax - and yet they are being punished by a savings trap which has not been changed for over 15 years. "There are credible solutions out there that would free young people a lifetime of expensive care costs, and it was deeply disappointing that the Government scrapped the reforms needed to do this back in 2024. "I am calling on the Health Secretary to engage with disabled young people like Maxwell and urgently put forward solutions to end the savings trap." Mr McKnight said the existing rules make it difficult for disabled people with complex care needs to build financial security despite being encouraged into employment. He said: "I've worked incredibly hard to graduate from university and build a career. As someone who's driven and determined not to let my disability define what I can achieve, it's incredibly difficult to accept that, in many ways, I could be financially better off being unemployed. "The government wants more disabled people in employment, yet the very system that's supposed to support us makes it almost impossible for those of us with complex needs to build financial security. "I don't want special treatment. I want the same opportunities as my peers to save for a home, build a future and enjoy the rewards of working hard." As part of the campaign, Mr Sollom has requested a meeting with the Health Secretary and has urged the forthcoming Casey Commission on adult social care reform to examine the challenges facing working-age disabled adults seeking to save money and purchase their own homes. The MP has also pointed to previously proposed reforms, including measures in the 2014 Care Act and recommendations from the Dilnot review, which would have significantly increased the capital threshold but were ultimately not implemented.

metadata.title: More than 50 Cambridgeshire foster carers honoured for 450 years of service
metadata.contentSnippet: More than 50 Cambridgeshire foster carers have been honoured for their service and dedication to children in care.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 50 foster carers have been honoured for their service and dedication to children in care. The awards ceremony, held on October 2 at Burgess Hall in St Ives, celebrated carers from across Cambridgeshire who collectively contribute more than 450 years of fostering. Councillor Edna Murphy, chair of the children and young people’s committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said at the event: "Tonight is about saying a huge thank you to our foster carers and recognising the incredible difference they make to children's lives. "It is often the quiet, understated things that matter most to children: being there to listen, helping with homework, providing comfort during difficult times and giving children the confidence to believe in themselves. "These moments may seem ordinary, but together they can be genuinely life changing and life enhancing." The Foster Carer Awards are organised by Cambridgeshire County Council to honour the impact foster carers have on young lives. This year, 45 fostering households were recognised for reaching service milestones of five, 10, 15, 20, and 50 years. The theme for the evening was Around the World in 80 Days, with guests arriving in colourful fancy dress and enjoying food, refreshments, and dancing. Many carers were praised for offering stability, encouragement, and a sense of belonging to children in care. The High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire, Francis Burkitt DL, said: "I feel very privileged to have attended the awards this evening and to have met so many impressive and loving foster carers and heard their stories. "The support, stability and encouragement they provide helps children and young people thrive, often during some of the most challenging periods of their lives. "Their commitment is truly inspiring, and these awards are richly deserved." Anyone interested in becoming a foster carer in Cambridgeshire is encouraged to contact the council’s fostering team.

metadata.title: Dazzling meteor shower from rare comet to peak in the UK this week
metadata.contentSnippet: The Orionid meteor shower, known for its fast, bright meteors, will peak in the coming week.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Dazzling meteor shower from rare comet to peak in the UK this week
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A dazzling display of shooting stars is set to light up the night sky in the UK this month. The Orionid meteor shower, known for its fast, bright meteors, will peak in the coming week. The Orionids are visible each year between October 2 and November 7. Here is how they can best be viewed in the UK. The Orionids are an annual event, towards the end of each year. However, they are considered "extra special" by many, as they are actually pieces of Comet 1P/Halley, famously known as Halley's Comet. As explained by the Royal Museums Greenwich: "A meteor is a piece of space debris that burns up as it enters the earth’s atmosphere creating a ‘shooting star’. "Certain times of the year are known for spectacular displays and these are generally associated with comets that have passed by after spewing fragments in their wake." While Halley's Comet only flies by Earth once every 75 to 76 years, the annual shower provides some compensation for those who may miss that once-in-a-lifetime event. Meteors from the Orionid shower can be seen with the naked eye from all parts of the sky, though they appear to originate from the constellation Orion. Stargazers are advised to find a dark, open area away from city lights. This year, the shower will peak on the night of October 21 and continue into the early hours of October 22. However, a waxing gibbous moon will add extra light to the sky on October 21, which could make the meteors harder to spot. Recommended reading: RMG says: "Hunting for meteors, like the rest of astronomy, is a waiting game, so it's best to bring a comfy chair to sit on and to wrap up warm as you could be outside for a while. "You will need to allow your eyes to adjust to the dark." No special equipment is needed to enjoy the display. Have you ever spotted a meteor shower before? Let us know in the comments below.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Replacement doors and worktops are transforming kitchens across the UK
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Brought to you by Joe's Doors A complete kitchen renovation has long been considered one of the most disruptive and expensive home improvement projects a UK household can take on. Weeks without a functioning cooking space, coupled with the expense of stripping out structurally sound cabinetry, often leave homeowners putting off improvements for years. That frustration has prompted many people to seek smarter ways to update their homes without the chaos of a full structural rebuild. Nationwide specialist Joe's Doors provides a practical alternative by focusing on what actually needs updating rather than tearing out entire kitchens. A fitted kitchen layout combining Mason Indigo and Light Grey cabinet doors with fresh worktops (Image: Joe's Doors) The business focuses on replacement kitchen doors, drawer fronts, and worktops, retaining the existing cabinet carcasses beneath. In many homes, the underlying cupboards remain in solid condition, meaning only the exterior surfaces need a refresh. By keeping sound base and wall units in place, the refit process substantially cuts down on both installation time and household disruption. It also prevents large volumes of reusable timber and cabinetry from being thrown into landfill unnecessarily. Customers can choose from a broad variety of door designs and finishes, ranging from classic shaker profiles to sleek contemporary handleless styles. Named styles include the Trenton, Ottawa, Mason, Jones, Horton, Hereford, Cutler, and Athlone ranges. These designs are paired with modern colour palettes, with shades such as Serica Taupe, Indigo, Porcelain, Kashmir, and Dust Grey proving popular among homeowners. The transformation is completed with durable replacement worktops, coordinated end panels, and modern handles to give the entire room a cohesive look. Rather than leaving customers to coordinate independent tradespeople, the company manages the entire refit using its own experienced professional fitters. Prospective clients can examine physical samples in their own homes through an arranged home visit, allowing colours and textures to be viewed under real lighting conditions. Kitchen cabinetry finished in Ottawa Serica Dust Grey (Image: Joe's Doors) Every project begins with an accurate survey of the room before doors and surfaces are made to measure. Because the existing frames remain undisturbed, installations take far less time than conventional full refits. To make kitchen improvements accessible, flexible kitchen payment plans are also offered to help spread the cost over time.
