metadata.title: Hinchingbrooke Hospital redevelopment takes major step with six-hectare land deal
metadata.contentSnippet: Plans to redevelop Hinchingbrooke Hospital have taken a major step forward.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hinchingbrooke Hospital redevelopment takes major step with six-hectare land deal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Plans to redevelop Hinchingbrooke Hospital have taken a major step forward. This follows an agreement in principle to acquire land as part of a major hospital redevelopment programme. North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust has reached agreement in principle to acquire around six hectares of former Cambridgeshire Constabulary land, which will be used to support the redevelopment of Hinchingbrooke Hospital. Deborah Lee, senior responsible officer for the Hinchingbrooke Hospital Redevelopment, said: "Reaching agreement on this land acquisition is a major milestone for the Hinchingbrooke Hospital Redevelopment Programme. "Securing this site will allow us to deliver the vital infrastructure needed to support our plans for a modern hospital that meets the needs of our patients, staff and communities for decades to come." The land will be used for critical infrastructure, including a new access road, around 682 parking spaces, environmental mitigation works, and low-carbon energy infrastructure. These improvements are subject to planning approval. A public exhibition showcasing the latest plans will be held in the Garden Restaurant at Hinchingbrooke Hospital on Saturday October 17 from 10am to 2pm. The project aims to address challenges posed by ageing hospital infrastructure and to support the healthcare needs of a growing population in Huntingdonshire and nearby areas. The acquisition is also expected to improve access to the hospital and reduce congestion in the surrounding area. Darryl Preston, police and crime commissioner, said: "As owner of the police estate in Cambridgeshire, I have a duty to ensure that land no longer needed for policing purposes is used in a way that delivers the greatest benefit to the public. "Once finalised, this sale will help improve access to local healthcare facilities, providing a positive outcome for residents and the wider community." The transaction is still subject to legal completion and final approvals. This includes the return of land to the police and crime commissioner from National Highways after the completion of the Views Common scheme.

metadata.title: Hunts leaseholder furious over 'unacceptable' bill increase and payment issues
metadata.contentSnippet: A Huntingdon leaseholder says he has lodged a complaint with Places for People after an "unacceptable" 90% bill increase and other payment issues.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts leaseholder furious over 'unacceptable' bill increase and payment issues
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire leaseholder says he has lodged a complaint with a major social housing provider after an 'unacceptable' 90% bill increase and other payment issues. Blazej Kalinowski, who rents under a shared ownership scheme with Places for People, said that his building insurance suddenly doubled with little explanation. When he signed up with the company in November 2024, he paid £20 a month in insurance on his two-bedroom property in Huntingdon. But he was surprised when this year the bill nearly doubled. Blazej said: "I understand that prices will go up every year as you can expect that. "However I was a bit shocked this year in April when it suddenly went from £20 to over £40." He claimed that the company Places for People get to manage the property also failed to collect his rent one month and the following month only took around £30 out of the full £500 bill. Blazej said: "The third month they took nearly £900 for two rents altogether. "I'm a single father who's coparenting two children, you can imagine on one salary it's a bit tricky these days. "Why do I have to chase about payments, why are they collecting money in random amounts whenever it suits them instead of as its supposed to be on the first of each month?" Blazej has raised a complaint with Places for People, but said the response from stage 1 was that they couldn't see any wrongdoing from the company. He added: "For me, a nearly double increase is completely unacceptable. "What worries me is that this may not just affect me, but thousands of people around the country because Places for People have a lot of properties. "At the end of the day, we are in such a financial state that everyone is looking for savings. "So this increase, I can manage it but it's a huge burden on my monthly expenses." Blazej has two children and the price increase and inconsistent rent bills are costs he would much prefer to spend on activities with them. He also fears the bills will continue to rise with little explanation. He said: "If I managed a property and I saw that my client would be paying nearly 90% more on house insurance from one year to another, I would question why that was happening and how can that be justified." Ben Obese-Jecty, MP for Huntingdon, raised concerns about Places for People with Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook in Parliament on September 7. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "I have received over 70 complaints from tenants in my constituency who are resident in Places for People properties about its failure to maintain its obligation to fix the property and carry out basic maintenance. "Are the Government aware of whether this is a more widespread problem, and is there anything they can do to encourage Places for People to fulfil its obligations?" Mr Pennycook responded that Places for People will have no doubt heard the complaints raised. He added: "Social housing providers are regulated on the basis of consumer standards, and they are inspected on that basis. "We have introduced Awaab’s law, which provides that landlords have to fix hazards within specified time limits. "If he wants to write to me with further information about the development in question, I will be happy to look into it." “We aim to keep service charges as low as possible but costs to run buildings - particularly insurance - are continuing to rise. A spokesperson for Places for People said: “At the start of each financial year, insurance charges are estimated using the best information available at that time. "Once the final premium is confirmed, a review is carried out to ensure customers are charged only the actual cost. "In this case, that review resulted in a deficit on Customers’ accounts. Due to the difference between the estimated and final cost, a shortfall arose and a balancing charge has been applied to customers’ accounts. “With regard to the Customer’s rent payments, we acknowledge that the issues they experienced did not meet our usual standards. "We are working closely with the customer to resolve these issues and can confirm that their account has now been updated.”

metadata.title: Eligible people across Cambridgeshire urged to get free NHS winter vaccines
metadata.contentSnippet: NHS Central East is encouraging people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough to check whether they are eligible for free NHS vaccinations and take up the offer to help protect themselves this winter.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Eligible people across Cambridgeshire urged to get free NHS winter vaccines
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: NHS Central East is encouraging people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough to check whether they are eligible for free NHS vaccinations and take up the offer to help protect themselves this winter. As we head into the colder months, viruses such as flu, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) spread more easily as people spend more time indoors and in close contact with others. These illnesses can lead to serious complications, particularly for older people, pregnant women, young children and those with certain health conditions. Vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to protect yourself, your family and your community. It can help reduce the risk of serious illness, hospital admission and pressure on NHS services during the winter months. This winter, a range of free NHS vaccinations are available to help protect those most at risk from serious illness: Flu vaccine: available for adults aged 65 and over, pregnant women, 2-3 year olds, school-age children, people with certain health conditions, carers, homeless people and frontline health and care workers. COVID-19 vaccine: available for people aged 75 and over, older adult care home residents and those with weakened immune systems. RSV vaccine: available for pregnant women, adults aged 75 and over, residents in adult care homes and people aged 65 to 74 with a weakened immune system or certain long-term lung conditions. Pneumococcal vaccine: available for people aged 65 and over and some people with underlying health conditions. Depending on the vaccine, eligible people may be able to receive their vaccination at a GP practice, community pharmacy, maternity service, care home or local vaccination service. People eligible for flu or COVID-19 vaccinations can book through the NHS App or National Booking Service and may also receive an invitation from their GP practice. People who think they may be eligible for an RSV or pneumococcal vaccine should contact their GP practice to check their eligibility and arrange an appointment. Cali Makewell, strategic vaccination lead for NHS Central East, said: "Winter viruses such as flu, COVID-19 and RSV can cause serious illness, especially for people who are more vulnerable to infection. "Getting vaccinated is one of the simplest and most effective ways to protect yourself and those around you. "We encourage everyone who is eligible to take up the offer of their free NHS vaccinations. By getting vaccinated, you are helping to protect your own health while also helping to reduce pressure on NHS services this winter." People can find out more about winter vaccinations, check their eligibility and learn how to book on the NHS winter vaccinations webpage Winter vaccinations and winter health - NHS.

metadata.title: Drunk man who sexually assaulted woman messaged victim to say he 'enjoyed' it

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire man who sexually assaulted a woman who had gone to check on his welfare has been jailed for five years. Richard Kemp, 57, of no fixed abode but of the Huntingdon area, attacked the victim when she visited him on May, 9 2023. Kemp was drunk and became verbally abusive towards her and when she attempted to leave, he grabbed her from behind. He pulled her hair and sexually assaulted her, then stopped and told her he had forgotten who he was attacking. When the victim again tried to leave, Kemp subjected her to a second sexual assault but this time she managed to flee to a friend's home. Afterwards, Kemp messaged the woman to apologise, but said he had "enjoyed" it. The following day, he sent another message which said: "On the good side, there is no time limit for sexual abuse. "So, if you ever do want to make a complaint, I shall capitulate." Five days later, Kemp, who was drunk, handed himself in at Parkside Police Station in Cambridge. He officers he had sexually assaulted a woman earlier that month. He was arrested but denied two counts of assaulting a woman aged 13 or over by penetration with a part of the body or a thing. Following a trial at Peterborough Crown Court in August, he was found guilty of both offences. At the same court on Thursday (October 8), Kemp was sentenced to five years in prison and placed on the Sex Offenders Register. DC Katie Housham, who investigated, said: "Kemp subjected the victim to a terrifying and degrading ordeal when she had simply gone to check on his welfare. "His actions have had a lasting impact on the victim, who showed immense courage in reporting the offences and supporting the investigation through to trial. "I welcome the sentence handed down by the court and hope it provides the victim with some reassurance that Kemp has been held accountable for his crimes." Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: 29 Filipino nurses mark 25 years of service at Hinchingbrooke Hospital
metadata.contentSnippet: A group of Filipino nurses have been honoured for 25 years of dedicated service at Hinchingbrooke Hospital in Huntingdon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 29 Filipino nurses mark 25 years of service at Hinchingbrooke Hospital
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A group of Filipino nurses have been honoured for 25 years of dedicated service at Hinchingbrooke Hospital in Huntingdon. The nurses, who first arrived in the UK in 2001, have spent a quarter of a century caring for patients and supporting colleagues across the trust. Many remain part of the workforce, having built careers, friendships, and families in the community. Menchie Lynn, clinical site matron and one of the original arrivals, said: "We've had a lovely time marking our 25-year milestone together. "It has been wonderful to celebrate. "The difficult and heart breaking moments were when we left our families behind. "But we are still glad to be here and serve the community of Huntingdon and Cambridgeshire." To mark the occasion, the hospital hosted an afternoon tea where nurses received long service certificates, commemorative badges, and vouchers. A special video reflecting on their journey over the past 25 years was also shared. Hannah Coffey, chief executive of North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust, said: "We celebrated not only the many years of service, but the countless lives that have been touched along the way and the lasting legacy that has been built. "Our Filipino nurses have cared for patients and families with dedication, compassion, and excellence through changing times." Of the 60 nurses who joined Hinchingbrooke Hospital in 2001, 29 stayed. Some have retired, while others have moved to different hospitals or abroad. Ms Coffey said: "We reflected together on the courage it took to leave everything familiar behind to start a new life in the UK. "This celebration is an opportunity to thank each and every one of them for their outstanding contribution to healthcare and to our Trust." Some of their children have even gone on to work within the Trust, continuing a legacy of care across generations.

metadata.contentSnippet: A debut novel exploring the boundaries of artificial intelligence and consciousness will be published on 27 October.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A debut novel exploring the boundaries of artificial intelligence and consciousness will be published on 27 October. Written by 21-year-old student Francesca Nicolaides, The Animator’s Code tells the story of a rogue AI and the emotional and ethical dilemmas that unfold. Francesca , from Alconbury, began writing the novel as a personal project and describes the book as a way of processing the rapid rise of AI in everyday life. She said: "For a long time, artificial intelligence felt incredibly science-fiction to me – something that existed in the distant future rather than something we would actually be able to speak to and interact with in our everyday lives. "Then suddenly, that future arrived." Published by Cranthorpe Millner, The Animator’s Code explores human-AI relationships, corporate control of autonomous technology, and the nature of consciousness and personhood. The Animator's Code book cover (Image: The Animator's Code) Francesca said she has always enjoyed creative writing but never expected to become a published author. She said: "When I began writing The Animator’s Code, I was really writing it for myself. "But something changed during the process and I became completely absorbed in it and couldn’t put it down. "At that point, I decided to take the chance and approach publishers." She is already working on a sequel and hopes the story could one day be adapted for film. Francesca recently began her studies at ARU Peterborough and said she is passionate about teaching as well as writing. She said: "In education, you have the opportunity to nurture children as they grow, help them discover what they are capable of and potentially have an impact that stays with them for years. "I’m excited to be starting Primary Education at ARU Peterborough and to see where both my studies and my writing take me."

metadata.title: Zoo experts warn visitor behaviour risk can never be eliminated after tiger death
metadata.contentSnippet: Risks can never truly be eliminated, zoo safety experts have said after a man was fatally attacked by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Zoo experts warn visitor behaviour risk can never be eliminated after tiger death
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Public safety is an “integral part” of standards regulating zoos in the UK, but risks linked to “unpredictable behaviour” from visitors can never truly be eliminated, experts have said. Concerns were raised after a man was fatally attacked by a tiger when he entered an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on Saturday. The incident took place months after a three-year-old boy was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure at Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire. Dr Campbell Murn, a former member of the government’s expert committee for zoos and a lecturer in Conservation Science at the University of Reading, said such incidents remain rare, but strengthened regulations could help mitigate risks further. He said: “There’s an enormous amount of effort that goes into the securing of public safety for people who are visiting zoos, in addition to the weight that’s given to animal welfare in those settings as well.” “So it’s certainly something that is a very big and integral part of the zoo standards in this country.” He added that, in zoos that have dangerous wild animals, enclosure design follows set regulations, and staff are trained in emergency responses. “Their training is updated regularly, and they have immediately known and very rapid protocols to respond to emergency incidences, whether it’s an escape in the zoo or whether in very rare situations like this,” he said. “There’s a lot more extensive safety systems involved with dangerous wild animals,” he said. “There’s very clear standards that indicate the size and height of particular enclosures for dangerous wild animals.” Registered zoos across the country undergo regular inspections to ensure compliance with the Secretary of State’s standards of modern zoo practice, Dr Murn added. While some of these zoos “probably need to come up to speed”, Dr Murn said he does not believe the incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park was contributed to by a safety failure. Flowers left at the entrance of Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster (Image: Dave Higgens/PA Wire) He said: “It seems that in this case it was not possible to get there before the visitor was injured and subsequently died.” He also said the question of how to mitigate the risk of a visitor entering the enclosure of a dangerous wild animal was “difficult”. “Even the most elaborate enclosure, if they really want to get in, they’re going to find a way,” Dr Murn said. “What could be changed is to prevent the ease with which that can happen.” “If it was made much more difficult, then that would minimise or reduce the risk further, but it’s never going to truly eliminate it.” He added: “There are some zoos in this country that I don’t think are up to standard, and the process of phasing those out or improving the standards in those zoos is slow.” “There is a process in place, but it can’t happen overnight.” “So, I strongly would support the strengthening of regulations further.” A park spokesperson has said the tiger who attacked the man is safe and well and will not be euthanised following the incident (Image: Dave Higgens/PA Wire) Dr Paul Rose, a member of the UK Zoos Expert Committee (ZEC) and lecturer in animal behaviour at the University of Exeter, said zoos do take into account risks linked to unpredictable behaviour from members of the public in their safety protocols. “Public behaviour can be unpredictable as we all know,” he said. “There will be mitigation in place, such as high fencing, stand-off barriers, signage and explanation and a code of conduct for how to behave at the zoo — and for visitors to take responsibility for their actions.” “Risk assessments will also be undertaken regularly.” “However, a risk of unusual human behaviour will always remain.” “The majority of visitors behave in a way respectful of the animal and environment at the zoo, but there is always a risk of rogue or unusual behaviour and this will continue to be risk assessed and part of zoo personnel training.” Yorkshire Wildlife Park remained closed on Monday as investigations continue into the death of the man. Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on October 10 when the man entered the enclosure. A man died after suffering serious injuries in a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park (Image: Dave Higgens/PA Wire) He was pronounced dead at the scene, South Yorkshire Police said, adding that his family have been informed. The three-year-old boy who suffered serious injuries at Johnsons of Old Hurst was discharged from hospital in late August. The Cambridgeshire zoo said in a previous social media post it was “alerted to reports that a child had allegedly been thrown into one of our crocodile enclosures” on June 18. A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder following the incident and was later bailed as police said he was “assessed as not being fit for interview”. Police were called to Johnsons of Old Hurst zoo in June after a toddler ended up in the crocodile enclosure (Image: Joe Giddens/PA) The suspect in the case reportedly has learning difficulties and had been on a trip with carers, and an investigation has been launched into his care. In October 2016, a large silverback gorilla escaped from its enclosure at London Zoo, with armed police called to the central London attraction while keepers desperately tried to recapture the loose animal. Visitors were evacuated and London Zoo later said they were “never in any danger.” Malcolm Fitzpatrick, curator of mammals at the zoo, described the escape of Kumbuka as a “minor incident” in which the male gorilla got into a secure keeper area that was not open to the public. At the same attraction in 1992, a man was mauled by a lion after he climbed into a fenced enclosure. He was airlifted to hospital with a “very deep chest wound” after zoo staff fired CO2 extinguishers and gunshot to distract the animals. Other examples include a string of incidents at zoos owned by the late conservationist John Aspinall, with five keepers killed between 1980 and 2000. Three were killed by tigers, two were killed by elephants and both keepers and visitors also suffered injuries over the years.

metadata.title: Cancer service celebrates 10 years as annual visits rise to 10,000
metadata.contentSnippet: A cancer support centre in Peterborough has celebrated its 10th anniversary.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cancer service celebrates 10 years as annual visits rise to 10,000
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A cancer support centre in Peterborough has celebrated its 10th anniversary. The Cancer Wellbeing Service, based at Peterborough City Hospital, supports around 10,000 people each year, up from 6,000 when it relaunched in 2016. Lisa Deacon and Rebecca Hardy, joint service managers, said: "We are so incredibly proud of the service we offer and the wonderful staff and volunteers who deliver that service. "The Centre has been supporting people in its current format since 2016, since undergoing a major transformation to meet the changing needs of cancer patients. "In the first year, we had 6,000 visits – and that number has almost doubled in 10 years. "We are a free service available without referral to anyone affected by cancer and hold hands with the Trusts cancer unit." To mark the milestone, North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust staff and volunteers were invited to a birthday breakfast as a thank you for their hard work and dedication. Professor Steve Barnett OBE, chair of the trust, said: "The Cancer Wellbeing Service and its wonderful gardens are a jewel in the crown of our services. "The feedback we receive from patients and their families is exemplary. "And while the building is beautiful, what is even more beautiful is the care and compassion shown to all the service users." The centre originally opened in 1992 as the Robert Horrell Macmillan Centre, operating primarily as a day unit for patients already receiving hospital care. It was purchased for £850,000 through fundraising efforts by the local Macmillan team, who later handed it over to the hospital. Today, the centre offers support to people living with cancer, including those newly diagnosed, in treatment, recovering, or experiencing long-term effects. It also supports families, friends, and healthcare professionals. Services include one-to-one and group sessions, information and advice, art therapy, complementary therapies, and counselling.

metadata.title: DWP State Pension Age row takes new turn as Government responds to campaign
metadata.contentSnippet: State Pension age verdict as Government rejects calls to let older workers retire earlier - but there is still time to push for parliamentary debate

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP State Pension Age row takes new turn as Government responds to campaign
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Government has rejected calls to lower the State Pension age in a major update to a petition arguing that older workers should be able to retire earlier to free up jobs for young adults. The campaign, created by Helen Grice, has attracted 16,749 signatures and calls for the State Pension age to be reduced so more young people can get a foothold in the jobs market. But in its response, published on October 12, the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said: “The Government has no plans to lower the State Pension age.” The petition argues that making people work for longer means there are fewer jobs available for younger adults who are struggling to find employment. It says lowering the State Pension age could encourage older workers to retire, giving employers the opportunity to recruit younger staff while allowing people who have worked throughout their lives to enjoy their retirement. However, ministers have defended the current approach, pointing to rising life expectancy and the financial challenges of supporting an ageing population. The Government said: “We are fortunate today that more people are reaching old age: life expectancy has risen rapidly over the past century, driven by breakthroughs in medical treatments and generally healthier lifestyles.” It added that men aged 66 in the UK in 2026 could expect to live, on average, another 19.3 years, while women of the same age could expect a further 21.9 years. The DWP said State Pension age policy must reflect the fact that people are living longer, with some increases necessary to maintain fairness between generations, protect public finances and ensure the State Pension remains sustainable. The response comes as the Government's Third State Pension age Review gets underway. The review will consider what State Pension age is appropriate for future decades, weighing up a range of evidence, including an independent report from Dr Suzy Morrissey. While ministers have ruled out a reduction for now, they also acknowledged the difficulties facing young people trying to get into work. The Government said around one million young people are not in education, employment or training. It said it is investing an additional £2.5billion by 2029 in the Youth Guarantee and the Growth and Skills Levy, with the aim of supporting almost one million young people and creating up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn. The measures include expanded Youth Hubs, more intensive support through Jobcentres, additional work experience and training, a £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant and a £2,000 apprenticeship hiring payment for employers. The plans also include a fully funded six-month job for long-term unemployed people aged 18 to 24. Recommended reading Despite the Government's response, the campaign is still open for signatures. The petition, titled Lower the State Pension age to free up jobs for young adults, was published on June 25 and will close on December 25, 2026. It has passed the 10,000-signature threshold required for a Government response, but has yet to reach the 100,000 signatures needed for it to be considered for a debate in Parliament. The petition's central argument is that allowing more older workers to retire could create opportunities for younger people who are currently out of work. The Government's response makes clear that it does not plan to lower the State Pension age, instead pointing to its youth employment measures and the ongoing review of the age at which people can claim their State Pension.

metadata.title: The one thing Brits can't stop talking about as autumn Budget draws closer
metadata.contentSnippet: New research reveals how long Brits spend talking about money, why 68% lose sleep over financial worries ahead of the autumn budget this month

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The one thing Brits can't stop talking about as autumn Budget draws closer
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Brits spend 20 hours a month talking about money, making personal finance the nation's number one topic of conversation ahead of the Budget. Household bills, spending habits and savings are among the issues dominating discussions, with people dedicating a further 15 hours every month to talking about the wider economy. But the figures also reveal the toll money worries are taking, with one in four adults (25%) worrying about their household finances every day. More than six in ten (61%) feel anxious about money at least once a week, while more than two thirds (68%) say financial concerns keep them awake at night, according to research from Utility Warehouse. The findings come as households await the Chancellor's Budget announcements later this month, with millions hoping for clarity on what changes could mean for their wages, savings and monthly outgoings. Keeping on top of household finances has become a regular part of everyday life, with the average Brit spending an hour and a half a week on financial admin. That includes checking bank balances, paying bills and moving money between accounts, as well as keeping an eye on energy costs. The research found that: With household budgets under pressure, these routine tasks can be an important way for people to track where their money is going and spot potential savings. Younger adults are increasingly using digital tools to keep tabs on their finances, with Gen Z more likely to turn to banking apps and artificial intelligence. More than half (53%) of Gen Z respondents use banking apps to monitor their money, while 14% use AI. Older generations, meanwhile, are more likely to check their bank accounts regularly, with 66% doing so, or write down their spending in a notebook, a habit reported by 18%. Despite embracing digital tools, younger adults are not immune to financial pressures. While 36% of Gen Z respondents said they had a clear budget to track their spending, 11% admitted they often struggled to stay on top of their finances. More than one in five (21%) said they had dipped into their savings to cover everyday spending. Recommended reading: The findings highlight how financial concerns extend beyond balancing the books, with many adults worrying about their finances on a regular basis. One in four respondents said they worried about household finances every day, while 61% experienced anxiety about money at least once a week. The fact that 68% said money concerns kept them awake at night also points to the wider impact of financial pressures on everyday life. With bills, savings and spending all competing for attention, the run-up to the Budget is likely to bring renewed focus on household finances. The research was released by Utility Warehouse as part of its Chancellor of the Home campaign, fronted by brand ambassador Cat Deeley.

metadata.title: £14m approved for 16 active travel schemes across Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: More than £14 million has been approved for active travel schemes across Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £14m approved for 16 active travel schemes across Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than £14 million has been approved for active travel schemes across Cambridgeshire. The funding, secured through the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority from the UK Government’s Local Transport Consolidated Settlement fund, will support 16 projects over the next four years. Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways and transport committee, said: "Active travel remains one of our top priorities, so I’m delighted we’re approved a programme today, supported by fresh funding from Active Travel England, which will benefit diverse communities across Cambridgeshire over the next four years and beyond. "Whether schemes are linking homes, schools, employment centres, leisure venues or travel hubs – when active travel is a reliable option for local journeys it leads to safer streets, less isolated and more interactive communities, cleaner air and better health." Among the schemes to receive funding are widening the existing shared-use path from Great Stukeley to Alconbury Weald, improving links to Huntingdon Station, and a shared-use path connecting the A505 to Granta Science and Technology Park. Other projects include a new footpath on Cromwell Road in Wisbech and an active travel route between Ely and Soham, which will connect to the National Cycle Network. The council also allocated £80,000 per year for its School Streets programme, which aims to improve walking and cycling access around schools. In a separate decision, councillors agreed to reallocate £890,000 in funding from the Whittlesford-Duxford scheme to a new crossing at the A14 Histon interchange, pending approval from Active Travel England and the combined authority. This crossing is designed to improve safety for students travelling between Cambridge and Histon, including those attending Impington Village College. A further £2.776 million in revenue funding has also been earmarked for behaviour change schemes, such as Bikeability courses for schools, adaptive cycle training, and community cargo-share hubs.

metadata.title: All we know after 'trespass' at RAF base in Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: Counter terror police are investigating alleged trespass offences at RAF Molesworth - here's everything we know so far.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: All we know after 'trespass' at RAF base in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire found itself thrust into the national spotlight last week after counter terror police revealed they were probing alleged trespass offences at an RAF base. Security patrols by Ministry of Defence Police at RAF Molesworth identified an abandoned vehicle at 10pm on Wednesday (October 7). Officers from Cambridgeshire Constabulary attended and further searches of the area later revealed a small breach in the perimeter fence. At 2am the next day, two men, aged 36 and 32, were arrested inside the base perimeter. Here's everything we know so far. The pair were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage and taken to a police station. They were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023. The Latvian nationals living in the UK have since been released on bail with strict conditions, it was announced on Friday October 9. Officers carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation. the abandoned vehicle was recovered by police and taken to a nearby location. While undergoing further searches, concerns over the vehicle led to the deployment of specialist ‘EOD’ officers to carry out additional checks. As a precaution, a cordon was put in place, which impacted local roads in the Glatton area, including part of the A1(M). However, after assessment by specialist officers, nothing of concern was found and all cordons were lifted. The incident is now being investigated by officers from Counter Terrorism Policing. Commander Helen Flanagan, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but there is nothing from our investigation so far to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week. "Our investigation continues and we are working closely with colleagues from the Ministry of Defence Police and Cambridgeshire Constabulary on this. "A key line of enquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity. “Meanwhile, I would encourage the public to remain vigilant and if you see anything of concern, then to contact police." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

Weekly Family Update - 
25.09.26 
Headteacher’s Update: Keeping You Informed About What Matters Most 
There are probably more exciting ways to appreciate the size of a school than through a 
practice lockdown and fire drill, but our first one of the year certainly provided a reminder. 
Watching more than 1,100 students move calmly onto the field, line up sensibly and wait 
patiently was impressive. It is no small exercise, and our students handled it exceptionally 
well. 
We have also been delighted to receive positive feedback about the start of Year 7. Families 
have told us that their children have settled quickly, are enjoying their lessons, and are 
coming home happy and enthusiastic about school. 
Parents have particularly valued the care, support and guidance provided during the 
transition from primary school, helping both students and families feel confident and 
reassured. Staff have also been praised for building positive relationships and creating 
enjoyable learning experiences that help students feel they matter and belong. 
One parent summed it up perfectly: 
     "The transition has felt successful for both our child and our family." 
Feedback like this reminds us of the difference a supportive and welcoming start can make. 
Thank you to all staff for the part they have played in helping our new Year 7 students settle 
so well into life at Abbey College, and we look forward to welcoming our prospective Year 7s 
next Tuesday. 
There is lots more to enjoy in this week's Bulletin. Thank you for reading, and please 
encourage other parents and carers to sign up, as this remains our main weekly source of 
news and information. 
Andy Christoforou, Headteacher

metadata.title: Couple who kept 'vulnerable' man prisoner in his own home pictured
metadata.contentSnippet: Two drug users who kept a man with mobility issues barricaded in his own flat for more than 12 hours have been jailed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Couple who kept 'vulnerable' man prisoner in his own home pictured
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two drug users who kept a man with mobility issues barricaded in his own flat for more than 12 hours have been jailed. Zoe Smith and Shane Rowe visited the man, who was known to them, at his home in Dennis Road, Cambridge, at around 7pm on February 22, 2025. The man opened the door and the pair rushed inside and blocked his door using a table from inside the property. At about 1am the following morning, the man tried to get up from his sofa but was told he “wasn’t going anywhere”. He was then was punched repeatedly to the face. Violent behaviour by Rowe was spurred on by Smith who encouraged his anger. The ordeal continued for a further eight hours, until 9am, when the couple moved the table away from the door and left to buy drugs. Once he was sure they had left, the panicked man fled to his neighbours for help. So as not to arouse suspicion, he returned to his home and a short while later Rowe and Smith also returned. Police were not far behind, and at 10am knocked on the door. The victim managed to open the door despite being shouted at by Rowe. Smith jumped out of the window and Rowe also managed to escape. Zoe Smith was found guilty of false imprisonment and theft (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Afterwards, the man noticed his wallet and phone had been taken. The man told officers what had happened and said he lived in fear of the couple. Rowe, of Crosfield Court, Cambridge, and Smith, of College Close, Edmonton, London, were later arrested. In police interview the pair, both 39, denied the offences and otherwise answered no comment. They stood trial and were found guilty by jurors of false imprisonment and theft. Rowe was also found guilty of assault by beating. The pair were sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on Friday (October 9) where Rowe was jailed for eight years and Smith was handed five years behind bars. Both were also given indefinite restraining orders preventing them from contacting the victim in any way. DC Jack Sillince, who investigated, said: "I can only imagine the terrifying ordeal the victim faced, and the fear that he felt for more than 12 hours when he was kept prisoner in his own home. "Smith and Rowe used his vulnerabilities and mobility issues to their advantage, and I hope their prison sentences give them chance to reflect on their appalling behaviour. "No-one should ever be treated this way and we will do all we can to bring those who act so violently and threateningly to justice." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Heroes who saved drowning man from Hunts river earn national award
metadata.contentSnippet: Two heroes who saved a man from drowning in the River Ouse in St Neots are to receive national honours from the Royal Humane Society for bravery.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Heroes who saved drowning man from Hunts river earn national award
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two heroes who saved a man from drowning in a Huntingdonshire river are to receive national honours for their bravery. Alidio Gomez and Jade Ursell, from All Aboard Boating in Eaton Socon, leapt into the River Ouse in St Neots on May 27. They were on a cruiser when they spotted a man and a teenager swimming nearby. When the man disappeared beneath the surface, Alidio and Jade jumped from the cruiser’s deck and pulled him back up. A nearby rower joined the rescue, and together they brought the man to the riverbank and onto a jetty. The man appeared not to be breathing in the water but began breathing and talking again on the jetty. He was conscious and sitting up when the ambulance arrived. Alidio and Jade are to receive the Royal Humane Society’s top life-saving honour, a Testimonial on Parchment, for their actions. Andrew Chapman, secretary of the Royal Humane Society, said: "This was a serious life and death incident and time was of the essence. "If the man had been under water longer than he was it is unlikely he could have been revived. "Fortunately the two award winners realised they had to act at once, went into the water, got the man to the surface and undoubtedly saved his life. "They richly deserve the awards they are to receive." Mr Chapman urged the public to nominate people who carry out similar acts of bravery. He said: "There are many incidents where lives are saved but those involved never receive the awards they deserve because nobody nominates them. "We appeal to members of the public to tell us about incidents where lives have been saved, sometimes by people who put their own lives in danger." Founded in 1774, the Royal Humane Society is the UK's leading national body for recognising bravery in saving human life, apart from honours awarded by the Crown.

metadata.title: MP calls for action as Home Office continues issuing animal testing licences
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty has called for renewed action to phase out animal testing.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP calls for action as Home Office continues issuing animal testing licences
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire MP has called for renewed action to phase out animal testing. Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty raised his concerns at the Conservative Party Conference during a meeting with Isobel Martin of Animal Free Research UK. They discussed the Government’s failure to deliver its manifesto pledge to phase out animal testing. MBR Acres, a facility that breeds dogs, specifically beagles for scientific, medical, and veterinary research in the UK, is in Mr Obese-Jecty's constituency. Owned by Marshall BioResources, it can breed up to 2,000 dogs a year and sells them to laboratories for testing. The MBR Acres site at Wyton is the focus of ongoing protests, highlighting concerns over animal welfare and the ethical implications of animal testing. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "MBR Acres continues to be a focus for campaigners as the Government continues to use legal action on individuals to prevent campaign interference against it. "The Home Office continues to issue licences for animal testing despite the Government’s pledge and publication of the Replacing Animals in Science strategy later this year last year." He also questioned the effectiveness of the Home Office’s Animals in Science Regulation Unit, particularly its lack of regular unannounced site audits. The concerns come ahead of a Home Office report on animal welfare failings in British laboratories. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "As an officer within the All Party Parliamentary Group on Phasing Out Animal Testing in Medical Research I will continue to raise these issues with the new Minister responsible for the strategy, Chris McDonald." Regular protests outside MBR Acres began after footage of beagles was obtained in 2021, with activists maintaining a presence at the site since July that year. In a previous letter to science minister Lord Patrick Vallance, Mr Obese-Jecty said replacing animal tests could take more than a decade and require action from government, regulators and pharmaceutical companies. MBR Acres has said it operates under Home Office regulations and that an ongoing High Court injunction remains in force at the site.

metadata.title: 'UK's Best Burger' winners to open new restaurant in Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: The Beefy Boys, whose burger was crowned the UK’s best in 2023, are set to open a new restaurant in Cambridge.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'UK's Best Burger' winners to open new restaurant in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A burger chain crowned the UK’s best are set to open a new restaurant in Cambridgeshire. The Beefy Boys plan to open their eighth restaurant on Bene’t Street, Cambridge, in the former BrewDog premises. The bar was among 38 BrewDog sites announced for closure in March 2026 after the brewery was acquired by US firm Tilray Brands. Up to 50 jobs are expected to be created by the new restaurant, with recruitment under way. The joint's Old Boy burger won the UK’s Best Burger title at the 2023 National Burger Awards. Anthony "Murf" Murphy, co-founder of The Beefy Boys, said: "Cambridge has an exciting and diverse food scene, and it’s been one to watch for us for some time. "We’ve been eyeing it up and when the former BrewDog site became available, we knew the time was right. The joint has previously won the crown of UK's Best Burger "We’re incredibly proud of how far The Beefy Boys has come. "Just over ten years ago we were cooking burgers in our back gardens, and now we are opening our eighth restaurant. "We can’t wait to bring what we do to Cambridge and become a part of the local community." The Beefy Boys was founded in 2011 by four childhood friends: Mr Murphy, Daniel Mayo-Evans, Christian Williams, and Lee Symonds. Their other locations include Hereford, Shrewsbury, Cheltenham, Bath, Oxford, Nottingham and Exeter, plus two food trucks travelling across the UK. The Cambridge restaurant will serve The Beefy Boys’ signature menu, including Beefy Boy burgers, loaded fries, buffalo wings and hard shakes. The restaurant will feature The Beefy Boys' signature menu Vegetarian and vegan options will also be available. The Beefy Boys use 100 per cent grass-fed beef from their Herefordshire hometown and support local suppliers. The team plans a signature Beefy-style refit of the former BrewDog site and aims to open before Christmas. Further details and the opening date are expected to be announced soon.

metadata.title: Passengers warned of rail disruption ahead of improvement works
metadata.contentSnippet: Rail passengers are being warned of disruption to journeys ahead of improvement work on the East Coast Main Line.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Passengers warned of rail disruption ahead of improvement works
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Rail passengers are being warned of disruption to journeys ahead of improvement work on a major railway. Trains will be diverted between Doncaster and Peterborough, with rail replacement coaches serving intermediate stations. The changes come into force on Sunday (October 18) while Network Rail carries out engineering work on the East Coast Main Line. Almost 670 metres of rail will be replaced near Newark as part of efforts to deliver more reliable journeys. Nearly 50 metres of drainage will be renewed at Grantham station to improve the resilience of the railway during periods of heavy rainfall. Repairs will be carried out to brickwork at Stoke Tunnel, south of Grantham, to maintain the structural integrity of the historical railway asset. Meanwhile, electrical components between Grantham and Bullpit Lane level crossing, Balderton, will be renewed and replaced. John Grainger, joint head of performance, LNER & Network Rail East Coast, said the updates will "help deliver a more reliable railway". "These improvements will help reduce the risk of infrastructure faults, improve resilience during severe weather and support smoother, more reliable journeys," he said. "We’re grateful to passengers for their patience and understanding while we carry out this essential work." A spokesperson for the train operators added: "These improvements are an important investment in the East Coast Main Line. "While the work is taking place, some services will be amended and journey times may be longer than usual. "We encourage customers to check before they travel and allow extra time for their journeys." The following services will experience changes as a result of improvement works: The 08.00 Bradford Interchange to London King’s Cross will divert via Wakefield Westgate. It will not call at Halifax, Brighouse, Mirfield or Wakefield Kirkgate. A rail replacement service will operate between Halifax and Wakefield Westgate. The 12.00 London King’s Cross to Bradford Interchange and the 15.43 Bradford Interchange to London King’s Cross will not run. The 10.00 and 13.00 London King’s Cross to Sunderland and the 14.30 and 17.30 Sunderland to London King’s Cross services will not run. All other services will divert via Lincoln with increased journey times. A reduced and amended timetable will be in place, with trains diverting via Lincoln. No services will call at Beverley, Cottingham, Retford or Grantham. An hourly service will run each way between Scotland and London King’s Cross, and one service every two hours each way between Leeds and London King’s Cross. These services will use a diversionary route between Peterborough and Doncaster, extending journey times by around 60 minutes. Rail replacement services will connect customers from Retford, Newark Northgate, and Grantham with Doncaster and Peterborough. From there, customers can connect onto rail services to other destinations. There will be no services to or from Lincoln. Rail replacement coaches will operate in both directions between Peterborough, Grantham and Lincoln. There will be no LNER services to or from Bradford Forster Square, Harrogate, Hull or Skipton. metadata.title: Drink-driver who crashed into stationary vehicle leaving man paralysed pictured
metadata.contentSnippet: A drink-driver who caused a crash that left a man paralysed and another passenger seriously injured has been jailed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drink-driver who crashed into stationary vehicle leaving man paralysed pictured
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drink-driver who caused a crash that left a man paralysed and a passenger seriously injured has been jailed. Samiul Islam, 25, was driving at speed along the A1307 in Huntingdon at around 12.40am on August 2, 2024, when he collided with a stationary Mercedes. The impact forced the victim’s vehicle almost 30 meters down the road before coming to a stop, despite the handbrake being on. The driver of the Mercedes was left paralysed as a result of the collision, and one of Islam’s rear seat passengers also fractured her spine and collarbone. When officers arrived, Islam provided a roadside breath test of 42 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath. This put him over the legal limit of 35 microgrammes. At Peterborough Crown Court on October 2, Islam, of Pipe Lane, Peterborough, was jailed for two years and six months. He admitted two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving. He was also banned from driving for five years and 10 months. Sentencing, Judge Matthew Lowe, described the injuries caused by the crash as “profound, life-changing and permanent.” Describing the man who was left paralysed, he said: "The impact of the crash goes beyond the physical injuries". He added that when handing Islam his sentence, he must consider “the emotional and psychological consequences for him and those that love him.” PC Peter Smith, from the force’s Road Policing Unit, said: “Islam’s driving fell far below the standards of a careful and competent driver, and has ultimately left one man with injuries that will affect him for the rest of his life. "The impact of this collision on both victims cannot be underestimated. "It has had a lasting impact on Islam's rear-seat passenger's mental health, and the driver of the Mercedes’ life, as well as those of his loved ones, will now change significantly – both of which are a direct result of Islam’s careless and dangerous driving. "This was a completely preventable collision, and I am pleased Islam is now off the roads and will be held accountable behind bars for his actions." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire women feature in film about global pelvic mesh scandal
metadata.contentSnippet: A new documentary channel has launched with a hard-hitting film about the global pelvic mesh scandal, featuring women from Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire women feature in film about global pelvic mesh scandal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new documentary channel has launched with a hard-hitting film about the global pelvic mesh scandal, featuring women from Cambridgeshire. The film, The Medical Mesh Scandal Ruining Women's Lives, tells the story of March campaigner Kath Sansom and shines a light on what has been described as one of the biggest patient safety controversies in recent history. Kath, founder of the Sling The Mesh campaign group, said: "Behind every statistic is a woman whose life has been irreversibly changed by a piece of plastic mesh. "Thousands were told this was the 'gold standard' treatment, yet many were never fully informed of the risks or the devastating complications that could follow. "Women raising concerns were treated as isolated cases rather than evidence of a systemic failure. "Many were dismissed, disbelieved or told their symptoms were unrelated to their implants. "Much of this was driven by marketing that rested on limited scientific evidence. "The consequences have been devastating." The short film features Ms Sansom and fellow March resident Gail McCourt, and was produced by an all-female team. It is the first release from MAZE, a new YouTube documentary channel dedicated to telling underreported stories with depth and care. The channel plans to release new films every three weeks, up to 15 minutes long. The documentary explores the scientific evidence behind mesh implants, regulatory failures, and the human cost of ignoring warnings. It also examines industry influence, patient safety, and the importance of listening to women who report harm. A parliamentary screening of the film will take place on October 14, bringing together MPs, academics, clinicians, patient safety experts, and those affected by mesh complications. The event will examine lessons from the scandal.

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire water leaks fill 86 Olympic pools every day, Lib Dems claim
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire Liberal Democrat MPs have criticised Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch after analysis claimed trillions of litres of water had been lost to leaks across the East of England since the early 1990s.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire water leaks fill 86 Olympic pools every day, Lib Dems claim
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire Liberal Democrat MPs have attacked Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch after analysis claimed trillions of litres of water had been lost to leaks across the East of England since the early 1990s. The criticism comes after Kemi Badenoch reportedly described water privatisation as a “success”, a claim local Liberal Democrats have labelled “complete nonsense”. Liberal Democrat analysis of Ofwat data claims leaks from Anglian Water and Cambridge Water have wasted enough water to fill 86 Olympic-sized pools every day since records began in 1992. Ian Sollom MP says residents are being left 'high and dry' by water companies. (Image: Ian Sollom) The comments came jointly from Ian Sollom, MP for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire, Pippa Heylings, MP for South Cambridgeshire, Charlotte Cane, MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire, and Cambridge prospective parliamentary candidate Cheney Payne. The politicians said the figures exposed decades of underinvestment in water infrastructure as Cambridgeshire residents faced supply cuts, low pressure and shortages at home. The group said they had heard from elderly and vulnerable residents affected by supply problems and claimed some had been left without adequate support or access to emergency water supplies. Charlotte Cane is the MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire. (Image: Charlotte Cane) Mr Sollom said he had recently met representatives from Cambridge Water to discuss ongoing supply issues across the county. He said: “Residents have been left literally high and dry as the water supply keeps being cut off altogether or the pressure is so low, they can’t get more than a trickle out of their taps.” Mr Sollom said he urged the company to improve customer communications and register vulnerable residents for priority support during emergencies. The Liberal Democrats said water security was becoming more urgent in Cambridgeshire, one of the driest parts of the UK, as housing growth is expected to accelerate over the coming decades. The politicians said in a joint statement that the exceptionally hot, dry summer may have caused more burst pipes, but leaks had wasted water for decades. They also questioned whether existing infrastructure could cope with population growth and planned new homes. The party wants water companies turned into mutually owned public benefit corporations, with profits reinvested in infrastructure instead of paid to shareholders as dividends. The Conservatives have not responded to the Liberal Democrats’ comments. The Government has previously recognised Cambridgeshire's water supply crisis while setting out plans for regional growth. An Anglian Water spokesperson said: "Leakage remains one of our biggest priorities and we know customers expect us to keep reducing it. "Leakage levels on our network are around 40% lower than they were at privatisation, following sustained investment in finding and fixing leaks. Between 2025 and 2030, we're investing £348 million to renew more than 1,100km of water mains across our region."

metadata.title: Man bailed after protest camp outside puppy breeding facility cordoned off
metadata.contentSnippet: A man has been released on bail after Camp Beagle, outside MBR Acres in Wyton, Huntingdon, was cordoned off.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Man bailed after protest camp outside puppy breeding facility cordoned off
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man has been released on bail after a protest camp outside a puppy breeding facility in Cambridgeshire was cordoned off. Police established a cordon around Camp Beagle, the UK's longest-running permanent animal rights protest camp, on Tuesday (October 6). The protest group has maintained a continuous presence outside MBR Acres in Wyton, Huntingdon, since the summer of 2021. metadata.contentSnippet: Two men arrested inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire have been released on bail while police investigate.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Two men arrested inside RAF Molesworth released on bail
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two men arrested inside an RAF base in Cambridgeshire have been released on bail while police investigate. The men, aged 32 and 36, were arrested at RAF Molesworth in the early hours of Thursday October 8 after being found inside the base perimeter. Both are Latvian nationals who live in the UK. They were taken to a Cambridgeshire police station before being released on bail with strict conditions. Counter Terrorism Policing London is leading the investigation, working with the Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) and Cambridgeshire Constabulary. At about 10pm on Wednesday, October 7, MDP security patrols near RAF Molesworth found an abandoned vehicle. Cambridgeshire officers joined them and the forces searched the site. Officers then found a small breach in the perimeter fence. Officers later found and arrested the men on suspicion of trespass and criminal damage. They were later arrested on suspicion of an offence under Section 4 of the National Security Act. This concerns entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK. Police have searched two addresses in the Peterborough area as part of the investigation. Officers also recovered the abandoned vehicle found near the base. Commander Helen Flanagan, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: “We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but there is nothing from our investigation so far to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week.” She said: “A key line of enquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity.” Police urged anyone who sees something that does not look or feel right to report it in confidence by calling 0800 789321. Reports can also be made online at www.gov.uk/ACT. The investigation continues in Cambridgeshire. Specialist explosive ordnance disposal officers carried out additional checks on the vehicle as a precaution, but found nothing of concern; a cordon affecting local roads, including part of the A1(M), was later lifted.

metadata.title: Seven road repair methods trialled on Cambridgeshire's peat roads in UK first
metadata.contentSnippet: Seven solutions to how to repair and maintain Cambridgeshire's peat soil-affected roads are currently being trialled along a Fenland highway.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Seven road repair methods trialled on Cambridgeshire's peat roads in UK first
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Seven solutions to how to repair and maintain Cambridgeshire's peat soil-affected roads are currently being trialled along a Fenland highway. The media were invited on Thursday to see how the trials aim to deliver longer-lasting repairs and better value for taxpayers’ money. Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of Cambridgeshire's highways and transport committee, Paul Bristow, the mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, joined representatives from the county council's project team and its project contractor, WinVic, to outline the work so far. Funded by the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority, the UK’s first trial of its kind is testing seven road-building techniques side by side to find the best solution for roads built on peat. Cllr Beckett highlighted the significant challenges peat soil roads, like the trial site in Upwell Road, March, cause highways authorities, pointing out that Cambridgeshire has around 1,000 miles of roads affected by peat. Fenland is home to 93 per cent of those roads, which is why the county council has selected the road in March. Seven 150-metre sections of road have been dug up, each for a different proposed solution. One section uses the current repair method as the control: plastic geogrid mesh is laid on the road surface, covered with road plainings and resurfaced with asphalt. Andy Harmon, framework manager for WinVic, the contractor working with Cambridgeshire County Council on the peat soil affected roads trial project. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The other construction methods being trialled are: This plastic mesh, known as Geogrid, is currently used in road repairs across Cambridgeshire and the country. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The trial will help identify which of the methods offers the best solution. Monitoring of Upwell Road will be carried out over three years using a variety of techniques, from gauges buried beneath the road surface to satellites taking detailed images to show any movement of the road surface, including sinking. Cllr Beckett said repairing a peat-affected road can cost up to five times more than repairing one built on other soil. Cambridgeshire Mayor Paul Bristow left on site in Upwell Road, March. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Not only that, but repairs last half as long as those carried out in other parts of the county. Cambridgeshire County Council receives no extra funding for the higher cost of repairing and maintaining its peat roads. Joshua Rutherford, the council’s head of asset management, design and delivery, said it needs £58.3m to maintain the status quo, but the Government provides £31.3m, leaving a £27m shortfall. James Chapman (left), project manager, with Joe McGilley, design engineer, holding a diagram showing the structure of one of the trials. (Image: Sarah Cliss) More money has been promised to tackle the repair backlog, but it will arrive over four years, with most coming at the end, leaving the council to find the cash upfront. It is hoped the trials will provide a better solution to the peat soil-affected roads, but which of the six options will prove the best is up for discussion, with those working on the site pinning their hopes on different methods. However, there was consensus on just how important the trials are to future maintenance of the county's roads, and satisfying residents fed up with negotiating undulating, pothole-riddled roads around Fenland. Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of Cambridgeshire's transport and highways committee, pointed out that a pint of peat soil contains the same amount of solids as a pint of milk. (Image: Sarah Cliss) This plastic mesh, known as Geogrid, is currently used in road repairs across Cambridgeshire and the country. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The council says peat-affected roads are contributing to an £800m backlog in road repairs across the county.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A business leader has been appointed as a Deputy Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire in recognition of her service to the community. Faye Holland, chair of the Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce board, will now support the Lord-Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, Julie Spence, who serves as His Majesty The King’s representative in the county. Deputy Lieutenants are selected from across Cambridgeshire and may represent the Lord-Lieutenant at civic and ceremonial events, community occasions and Royal visits. Faye said: "I am deeply honoured to have been appointed as a Deputy Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire. "Cambridgeshire is an extraordinary county, defined by its people, communities, businesses and remarkable spirit of innovation. "I am incredibly proud to have the opportunity to serve the county in this new capacity and to support the Lord-Lieutenant in representing His Majesty The King across Cambridgeshire." She is also director of The Cambridge x Manchester Partnership and founder of the #21toWatch Technology Innovation Awards. Her career spans technology, communications, entrepreneurship and economic development, and she has held a range of mentoring, advisory and leadership roles supporting entrepreneurs and growing businesses. Charlotte Horobin, chief executive of Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "We are absolutely delighted for Faye. "This is a tremendous honour and a fitting recognition of the energy, commitment and leadership she has brought to Cambridgeshire over many years. "Faye has an exceptional ability to bring people together across business, academia, innovation and civic life, and she is a passionate champion for the county and its communities. "On behalf of everyone at the Chamber, our members and the Board, I would like to congratulate Faye on this very special appointment. "We are immensely proud to see our Chair take on this important role." Faye will continue as chair of the chamber board alongside her other professional commitments.

metadata.title: Swimming pool plans for industrial unit refused over parking and safety concerns
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdonshire District Council has rejected plans to turn an industrial unit in St Ives into a community swimming pool, despite backing from education, health and swimming groups.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Swimming pool plans for industrial unit refused over parking and safety concerns
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Huntingdonshire District Council has rejected plans to turn an industrial unit in St Ives into a community swimming pool, despite backing from education, health and swimming groups. Spencer Smith applied to convert 1 Bramley Road from a motorcycle repair workshop into an indoor pool offering swimming lessons, water safety training, hydrotherapy, aqua fitness and rehabilitation. Council planners acknowledged the community benefits of the proposal but concluded that insufficient information had been provided to address concerns over parking, public safety, noise and site selection. In its decision notice, the council said it had not been demonstrated that the development could operate within the established employment area without causing amenity and public safety issues because of a lack of parking provision. Officers also said the application did not properly explain why other sites had been ruled out. A second reason for refusal related to a lack of information about the proposed air conditioning unit and plant equipment. Environmental Health officers said there was insufficient detail to assess whether noise could affect nearby homes. The third refusal reason was parking: the four proposed spaces, including one accessible bay, were not enough for staff and users and could cause overspill on nearby industrial-estate roads. St Ives Town Council objected over highway and pedestrian safety, parking, the site layout and public safety. But the report said Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways team raised no highway-safety objection. Four organisations submitted letters supporting the scheme. One of the strongest endorsements came from the Swimming Teachers' Association, which said there was an ongoing shortage of suitable facilities for lessons and training. It argued the pool would provide opportunities for swimming education, professional qualifications, fitness activities and accessible sessions for people with additional needs. Wyton-on-the-Hill Primary School also backed the proposal, saying similar small teaching pools were often better suited to helping children gain confidence in the water than larger leisure-centre facilities. The school said it would be likely to use a purpose-built St Ives teaching pool because it would cut travel times. A local physiotherapy practice said the pool could offer swimming lessons, water aerobics and hydrotherapy, while specialist hydrotherapy was limited locally. A Cambridgeshire Pilates instructor also backed the plan, saying demand for aqua aerobics was high and classes at One Leisure St Ives were oversubscribed. The applicant’s planning statement said the pool would tackle a waiting list of more than 100 children, create jobs and bring a potentially vacant building back into use. It also said the pool could create at least eight direct jobs, plus work for independent instructors and specialist providers. But planning officers said the benefits did not outweigh concerns about parking, public safety, noise and the lack of evidence for choosing the site. Planning officers recommended refusal, and the council rejected the application. The applicant, Spencer Smith, also runs the local swim school Splash & Learn, where he teaches children to swim.

metadata.title: Huntingdon Town Council given go ahead to fly Pride and Pan-African flags
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdon Town Council has won permission to fly the Progress Pride and Pan-African flags from its historic Town Hall balcony, months after it was criticised for displaying them without consent.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon Town Council given go ahead to fly Pride and Pan-African flags
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Huntingdon Town Council has won permission to fly the Progress Pride and Pan-African flags from its historic Town Hall balcony, months after it was criticised for displaying them without consent. The issue surfaced earlier this year when it emerged that the Grade II* listed Town Hall in Market Hill had been flying flags without the planning consent required under advertising rules. Huntingdonshire District Council has now granted consent for the two flags to be flown each year from the building’s existing balcony flagpoles. Huntingdon Town Council applied to fly the Progress Pride flag throughout Pride Month in June and the Pan-African flag during Black History Month in October. Planning documents accompanying the application acknowledged that both flags fell into a category requiring express consent before they could be displayed on the Town Hall. The council’s new Flag Flying Policy says the Progress Pride and Pan-African flags are "subject to planning consent". In supporting documents, the council said the flags were intended to celebrate nationally recognised cultural and community events and reflect the town's diversity, inclusivity and community values. Officials stressed they would only be displayed during designated commemorative periods and would not be permanent fixtures. A planning officer’s report said the flags would not harm the historic Town Hall, the Huntingdon Conservation Area or public safety. The report said the flags would use existing poles without adding visual clutter, while Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways authority raised no objection. No public representations were received during the consultation period. The approval covers the Progress Pride and Pan-African flags on the Town Hall’s projecting balcony flagpoles from October 2026 to October 2031. The decision gives the council formal approval to fly the flags after it came under scrutiny for displaying them without consent, as previously reported by the Hunts Post. The council’s Flag Flying Policy allows other flags, including the Union Flag, St George’s Cross and Huntingdonshire flag, to fly at scheduled civic and commemorative events. But flags without automatic consent must first be approved by the local planning authority. The council has previously clarified that, unlike the traditional Gilbert Baker Pride flag, the Progress Pride flag does not benefit from deemed consent under advertising regulations and therefore needs express approval.
